abstract:
Although large language model (LLM) agents reason effectively, their practical value in enterprise settings is often limited by how they interface with target software. This thesis studies the agent harness (the non-model infrastructure handling actions, documentation, state placement, observations, and error feedback) as a performance-bearing architectural variable. We evaluate three harness designs using a shared, seeded local deployment of Ardoq, an enterprise architecture platform: traditional tool calling (H1), programmatic tool calling (H2) via sandboxed Python execution, and an agent-native domain module (H3) that raises the abstraction level over the same execution runtime.

The evaluation benchmark consists of 24 read-only analytical tasks based on recurring enterprise architecture workflows. Each task defines a typed output contract verified objectively in real time against the deployment’s live Ardoq API. Seven repeated runs per task-harness combination yield 504 evaluation runs.

Shifting from traditional tool calling to programmatic execution (H1→H2) removes a major state-coordination bottleneck. H2 increases the mean task success rate from 39.29% to 91.67% (+52.4 pp). It also reduces mean total tokens by 66%, the final context window by 45%, and estimated model cost per run by 48%. The largest gains concentrate on graph traversal, metamodel analysis, set construction, and cross-source composition; on these tasks, H1 typically fails either by exhausting its turn or time budget as context accumulates or by returning over-inclusive answers.

Raising the abstraction level (H2→H3) largely preserves correctness while further improving operational efficiency. H3’s exact pass rate is 91.07%, only 0.60 percentage points below H2, with no median per-task difference. It reduces mean total tokens by 18.9%, the final context window by 10.3%, per-task model cost by 15.2%, and wall-clock latency is 11.5% lower. One possible reason for H3’s slightly lower success rate is that its domain-tailored interface exposes less exploratory data, which saves tokens but may also limit the agent’s ability and inclination to explore when needed.

The findings support programmatic tool calling as the default for compositional enterprise workflows when code execution is operationally viable. Traditional tool calling remains sufficient for narrow report-based tasks. High-level domain modules are a selective trade-off, justified when stable, recurring workflows warrant the governance and maintenance costs of the abstraction. These conclusions are limited to one frontier model, one seeded Ardoq deployment, and read-only analytical tasks.

chap:introduction:
1.1Motivation

Large language models (LLMs) have moved rapidly into workplace use. McKinsey reports a sharp increase in regular organisational use between 2023 and 2024, while Microsoft and LinkedIn found that 75% of surveyed knowledge workers used generative AI at work in 2024 [1, 2, 3]. McKinsey estimates that generative AI could add $2.6–$4.4 trillion in annual value across analysed business use cases, provided that organisations can adopt the technology and redeploy work effectively [4].

Realised value remains uneven. Few organisations attribute a meaningful share of earnings to generative AI, and many remain between experimentation and scaled use [2, 5]. Productivity depends not only on the model, but also on task context, expertise, workflow design, data, governance, and human–AI collaboration [6, 5]. For enterprise software, the LLM must be connected to the applications, data models, permissions, validation rules, and operating procedures through which work is performed.

The agent–system interface is therefore a central design problem. An enterprise agent must discover and parameterise actions, preserve intermediate state, and recover from errors. The agent harness, the non-model infrastructure between the LLM and target system, handles these concerns. Recent work supports treating this harness as an architectural variable: tool representation and composition can affect reliability without changing the LLM [7, 8]. Tool-use research also increasingly studies system-level reliability across multi-tool trajectories [9].

Efficiency is part of the same problem: token-heavy traces increase operational cost and can increase latency as observations accumulate. Model computation also has an environmental cost. MIT’s review of generative AI’s environmental impact notes that generative-AI workloads are contributing to rising data-centre power demand, creating pressure to improve the computational efficiency of training and inference [10]. Harness design affects both operating economics and the model computation needed for a workflow.

One response is to let the LLM write code that composes operations and retains intermediate state. Anthropic reports large token savings for this pattern, and Cloudflare uses typed code interfaces and lightweight sandboxes to expose large API surfaces [11, 12, 13]. These vendor reports establish practical interest rather than independent evidence.

Independent evidence also finds that executable Python can improve success and reduce action steps on API tasks [14]. Whether this generalises to enterprise platforms, which workflows benefit, and when domain abstractions are needed remain open questions.

Most code-execution approaches make an existing tool or API surface callable without changing its developer-oriented abstractions. This thesis also asks what operations, values, and domain concepts an interface would expose if designed for the agent. That question motivates the third harness in the comparison, which provides an agent-native domain module rather than a thin programmatic wrapper. The idea that an agent’s interface should be designed for the agent rather than inherited has begun to attract attention [15, 16]. It has not, however, been brought into a code-execution harness over a real enterprise platform, nor compared in controlled fashion against thinner code wrappers and the traditional tool-calling harness (H1) it is meant to improve. This controlled comparison is the central concern of the thesis.

Enterprise Architecture (EA) platforms such as Ardoq provide a demanding context for studying this question. EA platforms manage relational data through typed components, references, workspaces, reports, viewpoints, and metamodels. An agent must compose operations, interpret platform-specific schemas, preserve identifiers, and ground decisions in the Ardoq model governing the relevant workspace. Prior work on enterprise knowledge graphs similarly argues that LLMs become more useful in enterprise settings when grounded in structured relational representations rather than unstructured text alone [17, 18].

This thesis compares three agent harnesses: the Traditional tool-calling harness (H1), the Programmatic harness (H2), and the Agent-native domain module harness (H3). The model, tasks, and platform remain fixed. The controlled design stages two architectural contrasts: H1–H2 changes invocation style while preserving platform coverage, and H2–H3 changes abstraction level while retaining code generation as the execution mechanism. The study measures how these changes affect task completion, resource use, and failure behaviour.

1.2Research Questions

The research questions follow the two architectural transitions. Correctness, failures, tokens, and latency provide evidence for each.

RQ: How does agent harness architecture affect the performance and behaviour of LLM agents on enterprise architecture workflows in Ardoq?

This overarching question is addressed through three sub-questions.

SQ1: Invocation style. How does replacing the Traditional tool-calling harness (H1) with the Programmatic harness (H2) affect task success, failure modes, token usage, and latency?

SQ1 compares structured calls with generated Python over the same low-level Ardoq operations. It tests whether Python can retain intermediate state and compose dependent operations more effectively than turn-by-turn JSON calls. It is motivated by evidence that multi-step, sequentially dependent tasks stress the LLM’s ability to preserve intermediate state and compose operations across turns [19, 9]. If a programmatic harness helps, the effect should be clearest in tasks requiring iteration, aggregation, graph traversal, or conditional execution.

SQ2: Abstraction level. How does replacing a low-level programmatic API with an agent-native domain module affect task success, failure modes, token usage, and latency?

SQ2 compares low-level Python functions with an agent-native domain module while holding code execution fixed. H3’s operations encode recurring Ardoq and EA workflow patterns. Prior work on tool interface design suggests that the representation and composition of available actions can materially affect agent reliability without changing the underlying model [7, 8]. The question is whether domain-shaped operations reduce semantic misuse and state-management failures, or introduce new failures through abstraction mismatch, hidden assumptions, and maintenance burden.

SQ3: Task sensitivity. Which categories of enterprise architecture tasks benefit most or least from each harness architecture?

SQ3 examines whether architectural effects vary by task category and difficulty. Aggregate success rates can conceal deployment-relevant variation: an architecture that works well for report aggregation may fail on typed graph traversal or multi-source joins, and one that saves tokens on longer tasks may add overhead on shorter ones [20, 21]. The benchmark therefore records task tags and practitioner-rated difficulty scores to test whether architectural differences widen as compositional demands increase.

SQ1 and SQ2 test the two transitions; SQ3 locates their task sensitivity. Engineering cost informs practical interpretation rather than a separate research question.

1.3Scope and Contributions

This thesis is a controlled, single-platform case study. Ardoq’s typed components, graph traversals, and analytical assets make it a demanding testbed for agent–system interfaces. These characteristics reflect the complex information structures and analytical problems encountered in enterprise architecture. Ardoq’s active investment in AI-assisted features for enterprise architecture also makes the platform a practically relevant setting in which to study how LLM agents should interact with enterprise data. The author’s part-time employment at Ardoq provided domain insight into the platform and the challenges faced by enterprise architects, as well as access to a local development deployment containing a realistic organisational dataset.

The benchmark created as part of this thesis consists of 24 automatically verifiable, read-only analytical tasks. It targets compositional work that requires multi-step retrieval, traversal, filtering, joining, or aggregation while retaining an objectively verifiable answer. The tasks can provide evidence for a business decision, but do not ask the agent to make that decision. Each task defines a typed output model and a deterministic oracle that independently recomputes the expected answer against the live Ardoq API. This follows the objective-verification principle established by Agent-Diff for enterprise API tasks [20]. The suite excludes subjective assessment, generated-text quality, and LLM-as-a-judge scoring, making success traceable to platform state. The suite covers report discovery and aggregation, component queries, typed graph traversal, viewpoint execution, dashboard drill-down, metamodel reachability, parent resolution, recursive hierarchy aggregation, set operations, multi-source joins, and date-based partitioning. This follows the principle, established in prior benchmark design work, that aggregate performance scores conceal important variation across task families and that per-category analysis is necessary for understanding how harness design interacts with task structure [19, 21].

The thesis makes four contributions. First, it provides a controlled architectural framing of the agent harness as the unit of comparison. Prior work has mapped agent-system design dimensions and shown that tool interface representation affects reliability [22, 7, 8]. It has not, however, systematically compared different harness architectures across invocation style and abstraction level within a single enterprise platform. The staged controlled design provides a methodological template for comparing these realised architectural transitions while keeping the model, platform, tasks, and verification fixed.

Second, it provides an Ardoq-centred benchmark with objectively verifiable tasks. The benchmark’s task design is grounded in recurring EA workflows, including risk analysis, lifecycle management, process quality, capability management, infrastructure cost, data governance, portfolio aggregation, and vulnerability management. Each task is operationalised as a typed evaluation contract with a live-API oracle. The benchmark is architecture-agnostic: the same task definitions, verification conditions, and procedures apply to all three harnesses. Benchmark tasks are reviewed by human experts for their difficulty, usefulness, and frequency of use in typical EA workflows.

Third, it provides a comparative evaluation methodology for correctness, resource efficiency, and error behaviour. The evaluation uses repeated trials per harness-task combination to characterise both mean performance and variability. This follows the methodological principle that single-run task success rates systematically overestimate production reliability [21, 23]. It reports token usage, wall-clock latency, task success rate, and categorised error rates under the same LLM, task suite, and platform conditions.

Fourth, it derives practical guidance for enterprise agent integration. The guidance is scoped explicitly to the conditions of the experiment: a single frontier LLM, a single platform, and the final fixed task suite. The conclusions recognise the limits on generalisability. The guidance is intended to characterise trade-offs rather than provide universal prescriptions: which architectures fit which task conditions, where failures concentrate, and what engineering commitments each architecture entails.

The study does not attempt broad claims about all enterprise platforms, evaluate human usability, measure production reliability under sustained multi-user load, or compare multi-agent architectures.

1.4Paper Structure

Chapter 2 establishes the technical and domain context for comparing agent–system interfaces in enterprise architecture. Chapter 3 positions the study within existing research and identifies the gap addressed by the comparison. Chapter 4 explains how the comparison was designed and controlled, including the design-validation studies used to select the final H1 and H2 variants. Chapter 5 describes how the three harnesses realise this design and how they divide responsibility between the model and the interface. Chapter 6 presents the design-validation findings and the main harness comparison, then relates the observed differences to the interface designs and research questions. Chapter 7 answers the main research question, states the contributions and limits of the study, and outlines directions for future work.
chap:background:
This chapter develops the concepts needed for the comparison: tool-using language-model agents, locations of agent state, Ardoq’s graph model, and the compositional demands of enterprise analysis. It then defines the three harness architectures.

2.1Language Models and Tool Use

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network, typically based on the transformer architecture [24], trained to predict successive tokens and subsequently adapted to follow instructions [25, 26]. Instructions, interface descriptions, prior interactions, retrieved data, generated code, and final answers all enter the systems studied here as token sequences. The model consumes a bounded sequence, the context window, and generates a continuation one token at a time.

Token generation alone affords no direct access to external state: generating the name of a database operation does not execute it or reveal its result. Connecting an LLM to a database, service, or current platform value therefore requires a surrounding component that interprets a generated request, performs the external action, and returns an observation.

A common mechanism is tool calling, also termed function calling. The model receives specifications of the available tools and emits a structured object, typically JSON, that identifies a tool and supplies its arguments. An orchestrator validates the object, executes the corresponding operation, serialises the result, and appends it to the context as a new observation, as illustrated in Figure 2.1. Tool calling is related to but distinct from structured output: structured output constrains a model response to a declared schema, whereas a tool call is a structured request that the surrounding system interprets as an action. This thesis uses both mechanisms: structured calls mediate platform interaction, and task-specific structured outputs constrain final answers so that they can be verified. Schick et al. [28] showed that such behaviour can be acquired by the model itself: through self-supervised training, a model can learn when to invoke a tool, which tool to select, and how to populate its arguments, rather than relying on external logic to govern every decision.

Two properties recur throughout the thesis. The model acts only through an execution layer, and it can use only the operations and observations exposed by that layer. Its behaviour therefore depends on the interface’s names, descriptions, types, call representation, result format, and context cost as well as on the model itself.

2.2From Language Models to Agents

A single LLM invocation cannot adapt its actions to intermediate feedback. An agent embeds the model in an iterative control loop: the surrounding system assembles the task, interface description, and retained history; requests an action or final answer; dispatches the action; returns the observation; and repeats until completion or a stopping condition [26]. An agent is, in this operational sense, a model coupled to tools, state, and orchestration rather than the model alone.

In the classical taxonomy of Russell and Norvig [29], the evaluated systems in this thesis are goal-directed LLM agents (Figure 2.2): each receives a natural-language objective and structured target schema, then revises its actions in response to observations. They do not learn during evaluation or maintain an explicit transition model.

The idea of coupling model reasoning with external action has direct predecessors. Yao et al. [31] introduced ReAct, which prompts a model to interleave free-text reasoning steps with environment actions and observations; related work treats tool invocation as a learned behaviour [28] and equips agents to reflect on and retry unsuccessful attempts [32]. The harnesses studied in this thesis inherit the observe–act loop these works established, but realise it through tool-calling and code-execution interfaces rather than through ReAct’s textual prompting scheme.

The same construction supports coding agents that edit and test repositories [33], web agents that complete multi-step tasks [34], and API agents that select operations from large catalogues [35, 26]. Their performance depends jointly on the model and its interface. Wei [22] survey seventy public agent projects and identify the tool system, context management, and orchestration as recurring architectural dimensions whose design shapes behaviour independently of the model. The layer that mediates between the model and a target system is thus a subject of study in its own right; this thesis terms it the agent harness and examines it in Section 2.6.

2.2.1Locations of Agent State

An iterative agent needs information from earlier steps, but that information can reside in four locations (Table 2.1). Conversation state consists of task instructions, prior model messages, tool calls, and observations represented in the model’s context window. It is directly available to the model on a later turn, but consumes finite context and must be sent again as part of that turn’s input. Execution state consists of intermediate values retained by an external runtime, such as identifiers, report rows, or traversal frontiers stored in Python variables. It can remain outside the context window, but becomes visible to the model only when generated code reads it and prints a summary or result. Environment state is the authoritative platform data (in this case, Ardoq’s components, references, models, and analytical assets) which the agent can observe only through permitted operations. Finally, orchestration state records the progress of the control loop, including the current run, request count, retry status, and termination condition; it is maintained by the surrounding framework rather than used as task data by the model.

This distinction is central to the comparison. H1 carries intermediate results primarily in conversation observations, whereas H2 and H3 can retain them in execution state and compose dependent operations without returning every record to the model. All three observe the same Ardoq state under the same orchestration limits.

2.3Ardoq and the Enterprise Architecture Domain

2.3.1Enterprise Architecture and Ardoq’s Users

Enterprise Architecture (EA) describes and governs how an organisation’s business, data, applications, and technology fit together. The Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF) treats EA as both architectural knowledge and a method for developing and governing it [36]. EA representations support decisions about dependencies, change, cost, risk, and organisational transformation.

Ardoq is a commercial EA platform used by large organisations to document, analyse, and transform their technology landscapes. Enterprise architects are its primary users, while application owners, portfolio managers, risk and compliance teams, and transformation leaders consume or contribute to the resulting analyses. Rather than storing architecture as isolated records or static diagrams, Ardoq represents it as a schema-governed graph for querying dependencies, tracing impacts, and automating workflows [37]. Questions about change impact, incomplete ownership data, or aggregate cost and risk require traversal and computation across thousands of connected elements. This scale and connectivity challenge both human analysts and LLM agents. Figure 2.3 shows an example view of the Ardoq platform interface.

2.3.2The Ardoq Data Model

Ardoq can be understood conceptually as a directed, typed graph built from two element types:

  • Components are the nodes of the graph. A component represents any architectural element, such as an application, business process, technology product, data object, team, risk, or capability. Each carries system fields, including an identifier, a name, a type, and a parent field that places it in a tree hierarchy, together with model-defined custom fields such as owner, lifecycle phase, risk score, cost, or end-of-life date.

  • References are the edges of the graph. A reference is a first-class, directed, typed relationship from a source component to a target component, for example an application that is supported by a server. References carry their own identifiers and fields and may cross workspace boundaries, linking elements that belong to different domains.

Connecting components through references yields the instance graph: the concrete applications, servers, risks, controls, capabilities, and other components recorded for an organisation. Questions about dependencies, change impact, or ownership are answered by traversing this graph. Two further constructs organise and govern it:

  • Workspaces partition the graph into named groupings of related components, such as Applications, Infrastructure, or Business Capabilities. Because references frequently cross workspace boundaries, the overall graph remains connected across these domains.

  • Models form the metamodel or schema layer that governs each workspace. A model defines which component types, reference types, hierarchy rules, and custom fields are valid, so the vocabulary of types and fields is defined per model rather than globally. The metamodel can itself be viewed as a schema graph: its nodes are types rather than concrete components, and its edges describe the relationship patterns permitted between them.

On top of this graph, Ardoq provides higher-level analytical assets that package common query and presentation patterns, so that users need not traverse the graph by hand. Three are central to this thesis:

  • Reports are filterable tabular views over the graph. A report defines typed columns, server-side filters, and aggregations, and returns the rows that match its query.

  • Dashboards are monitoring views that compose several report-backed widgets into a single summary, aggregating data for an at-a-glance portfolio or status overview.

  • Viewpoints are reusable graph-traversal templates. A viewpoint specifies a starting component type and a path of typed references and, when executed from a seed component, returns the components, references, and workspaces it reaches.

Figure 2.4 summarises these layers: analytical assets query or traverse the instance graph, while the instance graph conforms to a metamodel that defines valid component types, reference types, and fields.

As Figure 2.4 indicates, these assets provide two levels of access: low-level traversal over components and references, and higher-level queries through reports, dashboards, and viewpoints. The harness determines how the model reaches each level.

Consider a recurring lifecycle-impact question: which servers support applications scheduled to retire within the next twelve months, where no successor application is planned, and what are those servers’ hosting types and lifecycle phases? Answering it requires more than finding one record. The application and server types and their relevant lifecycle fields must be identified in the governing metamodel; candidate applications must be filtered by dates and successor status; directed support relationships must be followed from the matching applications to infrastructure components, potentially across workspace boundaries; and the returned server identifiers must be enriched with fields needed for the answer. The final result may be compact even though producing it requires several dependent retrieval and computation stages. This example recurs below because it makes the interface consequences of state placement, programmatic composition, and domain abstraction concrete.

Ardoq also packages recurring customer objectives as Solution Guides: curated, pre-configured assets for specific business outcomes [39]. These guides are curated by Ardoq’s internal enterprise architecture experts. Examples include application rationalisation, application risk management, capability modelling, application hosting, and regulatory or operational compliance workflows. These solutions introduce and configure the practical artifacts through which users work with a use case: metamodels, reports, dashboards, viewpoints, custom fields, and other analytical assets. Figure 2.5 shows an example from the Application Rationalization Solution. Its executive dashboard turns portfolio data into a decision-oriented view of opportunity size and financial return, while its bubble-chart viewpoint visualises applications in the TIME framework: Tolerate, Invest, Migrate, or Eliminate, according to business value and technical fit [40].

The local development dataset combines these solution-oriented assets in one seed environment, approximating an Ardoq organisation in which several use cases coexist. Table 2.2 reports the scale of the local development instance used to ground the platform context in this thesis. The instance holds thousands of components and references across dozens of component and reference types, and most references connect components in different domains, so that cross-domain traversal is the norm rather than the exception.

Three properties make Ardoq demanding for LLM agents. First, graph analysis is sequentially dependent: each traversal result can determine the next operation, so difficulty depends on path depth and branching. Second, the platform offers layered abstractions, from primitive graph access to reports and viewpoints, and the agent must choose the appropriate layer. Third, reliable action requires metamodel grounding: model-defined types, relationships, and fields must replace generic assumptions about labels such as “application” or “business capability” [17, 18, 41]. These properties distinguish Ardoq from standardised, single-domain benchmarks. At the time of the study, there was no standardised benchmark suite for evaluating LLM agents on Ardoq or on enterprise-architecture platform workflows more broadly. The task suite developed in this thesis therefore has a dual role: it is the experimental instrument used to compare the three harnesses, and it is itself a deliverable that operationalises complex but objectively verifiable Ardoq analytical work.

2.3.3Agents in Ardoq

Ardoq already operates production LLM agents for an embedded chatbot, insight panels, and natural-language search. A dedicated AI service between the backend and the model implements the tool-calling pattern from Section 2.1. The service runs the agent loop through an agent framework called Pydantic AI, routes model inference through an internal gateway, and exposes Ardoq operations to the model as typed tool functions whose JSON parameter schemas are generated from their signatures. The model therefore sees ordinary tool definitions, while each function’s implementation calls back into Ardoq’s REST API to retrieve enterprise architecture data on demand. Agents have no durable memory between independent user requests. Within a request, prior messages remain available through the conversation context and the agent can query current platform data again; information used to continue the interaction must be present in or derivable from those sources. Operations execute under the requesting user’s credentials, restricting them to data that user is authorised to access.

In addition to one monolithic agent, the platform runs a catalogue of task-scoped agents that share this tool surface. A general-purpose assistant has access to the full set of operations, while narrower agents are restricted to the tools relevant to a single analytical asset. For example, a report-scoped agent is limited to report operations, with dashboard, viewpoint, and metamodel-scoped agents defined the same way. Scoping an agent to a task is therefore largely a matter of restricting its tool set. Every agent declares a structured output type that the model must populate, so responses reach the calling code as validated objects rather than free text. The same tool functions are also exposed through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. MCP is an open client–server protocol through which compatible AI applications can discover and use server-provided tools, resources, and prompts through a standard message interface [42]. Ardoq’s server thereby lets external assistants query Ardoq data without going through the Ardoq frontend [43].

This infrastructure supplies the H1 baseline and the common API foundation for all three harnesses. The open question is whether turn-by-turn tool calling remains suitable for larger graph analyses, or whether code execution and domain-shaped abstractions work better.

Pre-Existing Agent Tools

The production agents draw on a shared library of typed tool functions, organised into domain modules that mirror Ardoq’s analytical domains. Table 2.3 lists this pre-existing tool set and the purpose of each domain. Each function exposes only its domain parameters to the model, while authentication, the deployment URL, and logging are injected by the framework and never appear in the tool schema. The same functions underlie all of the task-scoped agents described above, which differ only in the subset they are permitted to call.

The catalogue in Table 2.3 contains 17 pre-existing production tools. For the experiment, this surface was expanded to 20 low-level analytical operations by adding broader component-query capabilities and the metamodel operations needed by the benchmark. The final experimental catalogue is documented in Chapter 4; H1 presents those operations as JSON tool schemas, while H2 exposes the same low-level coverage through a programmatic interface.

2.4Compositional Demands of Enterprise Analysis

Output size does not determine the difficulty of an enterprise analytical task. A short answer may require a long chain of discovery, retrieval, traversal, and computation, while one request may return a large report. Table 2.4 defines five dimensions of interaction burden. They overlap and are not independent experimental variables, but serve as a useful conceptual model of typical workflows.

Dependency depth concerns parameter flow, while fan-out captures repeated work over collections or graph branches. Intermediate-data volume separates processed data from answer size. Local computation covers deterministic transformations such as grouping, ranking, aggregation, and set operations. Schema discovery precedes these operations when the agent must resolve the platform constructs that express the user’s terms.

The lifecycle-impact example exhibits all five dimensions despite its small final answer. It requires schema discovery, dependent retrieval and traversal, fan-out across applications and servers, retained identifiers, and local date filtering. The dimensions suggest where harness effects may differ: H1 faces sequential and observation pressure, H2 adds programmatic iteration and computation, and H3 can encode recurring coordination patterns. These are design expectations, not findings; Chapter 6 tests whether the measured behaviour follows them.

2.5Interaction Scale and Code-Execution Agents

Tool-calling interfaces face four scaling pressures on such workflows: operation descriptions consume context, observations enlarge the history, dependencies require model round trips, and joins or aggregations require computational infrastructure. Longer histories can increase token cost and latency and can make relevant information harder for the model to use reliably [44, 45].

In the basic tool-calling pattern, a result is serialised into the context before the model selects its next dependent action. This does not require returning an unbounded raw response: pagination, server-side filtering and aggregation, truncation, or compact serialisation can reduce observation size. Those mitigations do not remove the underlying dependency, however, and they require the interface designer or the model to decide which information can safely be omitted. The lifecycle-impact example still requires the model to carry the application or server identifiers needed by later stages, even if each individual response is compact.

One response to this issue is to let the model write code that invokes operations, retains intermediate data, performs local computation, and prints only what the model or final answer needs. For the lifecycle example, one program can filter applications, traverse to servers, enrich them, and assemble the answer without returning each intermediate collection to the conversation. This can reduce model round trips and observation volume, but the benefit is not automatic: programmatic interfaces also require API documentation in context and can incur code-generation, execution, debugging, and error-reporting overhead.

Industry systems have adopted this pattern to manage large tool catalogues and intermediate data. Anthropic reports a substantial token reduction in a multi-system workflow, while Cloudflare’s Code Mode exposes an API surface through a typed programming interface [11, 12]. These are vendor reports rather than controlled studies. Independent work nevertheless shows that executable actions can improve success and reduce action steps in API-centric settings, and that programs provide variables, loops, conditionals, and multi-call composition [14, 46, 47].

Most code-execution approaches wrap an existing tool or API surface without changing its operation boundaries. This raises two questions: whether programmatic composition over low-level operations helps, and whether abstractions designed around recurring agent burdens help further. These questions distinguish the harnesses introduced next.

Note that executing model-generated code creates a security boundary involving credentials, process isolation, filesystem and network access, resource limits, session separation, and audit logging. This paper does not address these properties. Its execution service is experimental infrastructure, not a production-grade sandbox; deployment would require separate security assessment and hardening.

2.6Three Agent Harness Architectures

In this thesis, the agent harness is the execution layer between a language-model reasoning core and an operational environment. It determines the available actions, their description and invocation format, state handling, observations, and failure feedback. This usage follows emerging agent-systems terminology, in which an “agent harness” denotes the infrastructure for tool mediation, context handling, and execution boundaries, distinct from both the base model and any application-level framework [22]. The harness is an architectural variable: holding the model fixed and changing the harness changes what the agent can perceive, compose, validate, and recover from. Figure 2.6 locates six responsibilities between the reasoning core and the Ardoq platform: action space, interface description and discovery, invocation format, state handling, observation format, and failure handling, which represent different design dimensions of the boundary.

The three harnesses are interface designs over the same Ardoq analytical API, positioned in the two-dimensional design space shown in Figure 2.7. The horizontal axis is invocation style, ranging from traditional tool calling, in which the model emits structured calls whose results it can act on only after they return, to code execution, in which it writes programs that the harness runs. The vertical axis is abstraction level. A low-level operation corresponds closely to one platform capability and leaves sequencing, batching, identifier management, traversal, and post-processing to the caller. A higher-level domain operation packages recurring sequences, names concepts in domain vocabulary, normalises representations, or enforces invariants. Such an abstraction can reduce the number of coordination decisions required of generated code, but it can also conceal lower-level work, reduce observability, encode assumptions that fit some tasks poorly, and create maintenance obligations as the underlying platform changes.

H1 uses traditional tool calling over low-level operations; H2 exposes the same coverage through code; and H3 retains code execution but raises the abstraction to an agent-native domain module. The H1–H2 contrast addresses SQ1, and H2–H3 addresses SQ2. State placement, documentation, validation, error feedback, and observation handling vary with these realised architectures. The fourth corner of the design space (a high-level domain interface invoked through traditional tool calls) is not evaluated. The study therefore compares two neighbouring transitions, H1 to H2 and H2 to H3. It does not test every possible combination of invocation style and abstraction level, so its conclusions only concern these two realised transitions.

For clarity, Agent-native is an operational design term, not a claim of superiority. An agent-native interface selects operation boundaries, return structures, and composition mechanisms around recurring agent reasoning and coordination burdens instead of inheriting them from a human- or developer-facing API. The term is consistent with emerging work on agent-first tool interfaces [15]; the specific Ardoq domain module evaluated here is one implementation of that broader design stance. In this paper, domain-module harness refers to this concrete agent-native H3 implementation. SDK (Software Development Kit) is also used to refer to the domain-module.

Table 2.5 shows how the architectures distribute work among the conversation, execution environment, and reusable interface layer. Their schemas, references, names, types, and examples are part of the agent–system interface because they affect what the model can discover and use.

H1: traditional tool-calling harness.

H1 exposes Ardoq operations as JSON-schema tools and returns each validated call as a conversation observation. Schema validation can catch missing fields, invalid enumerations, and type errors before they reach the platform, while explicit calls provide action-level traceability [7]. Its principal limitation for this study is composition cost. The model can batch several independent calls in a single turn (called parallel tool calling), but it cannot use one call’s result within the same turn: any operation that depends on an earlier identifier, value, or schema must wait for a separate turn. In the lifecycle example, application discovery and filtering must return before their identifiers can parameterise traversal, and server identifiers must return before enrichment. Each dependent stage therefore adds another model round trip and carries relevant state forward in the conversation.

H2: programmatic tool calling.

H2 keeps the same operations but lets the model write Python that chains calls, retains results, performs local computation, and prints selected output from a sandbox. This is the code-execution paradigm of Section 2.5 applied to Ardoq. A single H2 program can filter the lifecycle applications, preserve their identifiers, traverse to servers, enrich the server records, and assemble an answer while retaining intermediate collections in execution state. This can reduce model round trips and keep large intermediate data out of the context. The cost is a broader failure surface and more execution infrastructure: generated code can fail at parsing, import, runtime, or semantic levels, so the harness must provide a sandbox, error feedback, and retry handling. Whether the compositional capability outweighs its documentation, execution, and repair overhead is an empirical question.

H3: agent-native domain module.

H3 keeps H2’s code-execution mechanism but replaces its low-level primitives with declarative queries, filtered reports, metamodel-aware operations, normalised subgraphs, and chainable traversal. For the lifecycle example, a query abstraction can combine type resolution, filtering, batching, and record hydration, while a traversal abstraction can preserve and advance the frontier across typed relationships. This is a form of semantic compression: recurring platform coordination is represented by fewer, domain-named operations in generated code. The compression does not remove the work; it moves it into reusable implementation and can make lower-level calls less visible. Its operation boundaries, names, and return formats encode assumptions that may fit some tasks poorly, hide platform detail, or overfit the benchmark and current dataset. The domain module also creates a larger maintenance surface than a thin wrapper. H3 therefore tests one concrete agent-native design, not the proposition that higher abstraction is universally beneficial.
chap:related-work:
This chapter reviews five strands of work relevant to agent–system interfaces: tool use, code generation, state and domain abstraction, enterprise automation, and executable-agent benchmarks. Together they expose the gap addressed here: a controlled comparison of harness architectures within one schema-governed EA platform.

3.1LLM Agents and Tool Use

Tool use lets an LLM emit commands, observe API or function results, and adapt later actions [31, 28]. The interface determines which operations the model sees, how it invokes them, and how errors return.

Early work established the main patterns for tool-augmented models. Schick et al. [28] showed that a language model could learn when to insert API calls, which API to call, and which arguments to provide from concise textual descriptions. Yao et al. [31] introduced the complementary pattern of interleaving reasoning traces with actions and observations, giving the model a way to track intermediate state and adapt to environmental feedback. This thought–act–observe loop informs all three harnesses in this thesis, each of which defines how the model acts and incorporates observations.

Later work showed that tool documentation quality materially affects reliability. Patil et al. [35] found that API-call errors often arise from hallucinated API names or incorrect argument signatures, not only from task reasoning failures. This is especially relevant in enterprise systems, where operations are numerous, documentation is uneven, and a plausible but incorrect call can modify the wrong platform object.

Controlled studies have begun to isolate tool specification format as an experimental variable. Sigdel and Baral [7] compare free-form documentation, JSON Schema, and JSON Schema with validation diagnostics while holding tool semantics and scaffold constant. Schema-based representations reduce interface misuse, meaning calls that violate the declared input contract, but not semantic misuse, meaning schema-valid calls that do not advance the task. This distinction maps onto the thesis harnesses: H1 constrains calls through JSON schemas, H2 through typed client functions, and H3 through higher-level domain operations intended to reduce invalid calls and poorly chosen valid calls.

At the system level, Wei [22] identifies tool systems, orchestration, context management, safety, and subagent architecture as recurring design dimensions across 70 public agent projects. This study uses the term registry-oriented tools to denote a finite catalogue of named tools whose signatures, schemas, or descriptions are registered with the agent before inference. The model selects its actions from this catalogue during execution. Protocol-based approaches such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) are gaining adoption, but they still require choices about which operations to expose and how to describe them to the model. This supports treating harness design as an architectural variable.

The field now pays more attention to multi-tool reliability over longer trajectories, not only isolated call correctness. Xu et al. [9] frame current work around planning, trajectory construction, safety, efficiency, open-environment capability, and benchmark design, arguing that the main challenge is now system-level reliability of tool chains. Wu et al. [8] show the practical importance of interface design: their Thinker framework improves τ-bench retail success from 68.3% to 82.6% with GPT-4o and from 49.6% to 81.9% with Llama-3.1 405B by adding state-machine-augmented tool interfaces without fine-tuning. Stateful benchmarks such as ToolSandbox further show that performance degrades when tools have state dependencies and conversational context must be maintained [45].

3.2Code Generation for System Interaction

An alternative to structured tool calling is programmatic tool use: the model writes executable code, typically Python, against a client library rather than selecting one operation from a static schema. This changes both expressive power and failure modes. Tool calling emits fixed-schema operations whose outputs the model can only consume on a subsequent turn. Generated code can instead combine loops, conditionals, data transformations, and multiple API calls in a single program, each able to use the results of the last [46].

Liang et al. [46] introduced generated code as an action representation for robot control, showing that language models could compose low-level skill primitives into hierarchical policies. The important insight for this thesis is not robotics-specific: code gives the model variables, control flow, and reusable intermediate results, which are difficult to express through isolated tool calls. Gao et al. [47] made a similar point for mathematical reasoning. In Program-Aided Language Models, the LLM generates Python code and delegates computation to an interpreter; on GSM8K this improved accuracy from 58.8% with chain-of-thought prompting to 80.0%. The gain came from changing the output representation and execution substrate, not the model.

Once generated code enters the agent loop, the scaffold becomes part of the reasoning system. Huang and others [48] show that language-model plans can fail when the model lacks grounded knowledge of available operations. Wang, Wang, and others [49] find that the interaction scaffold, including error handling and feedback structure, can create larger performance gaps than model choice in multi-turn tool-use settings. Deng and others [33] similarly show that software-engineering agents benefit from executing generated code, observing errors, and iterating. For H2 and H3, the sandbox, API documentation, exception messages, and retry policy are part of the harness being evaluated.

Code generation changes agent architecture, not only syntax. Trooskens et al. [50] propose a compiled-AI paradigm in which an LLM generates executable workflows once and later runs them deterministically without further inference, reducing token use substantially for repeated tasks. The thesis does not target such high-frequency compiled workflows, but the result illustrates the broader design space opened by code: determinism, amortised generation cost, and access to static analysis. H2 occupies a middle ground: it retains per-task generation while gaining the compositional advantages of code.

Felendler et al. [51] formalise this distinction at the protocol level. They compare context-coupled execution, where tool schemas, calls, and outputs are serialised into the model context at each turn, with context-decoupled execution, where the model generates a self-contained program that orchestrates the required operations and returns only the final result. Their CE-MCP architecture reduces token use, latency, and turn count while maintaining comparable task quality, but it also introduces new security risks because tool outputs and exception messages can influence executable code. Their results also show that the relative advantage depends on dependency structure: code handles linear chains and fan-out well, while stepwise tool use remains useful for adaptive loops and subjective filtering. This contingency matters for Ardoq tasks, which include both linear retrieval and multi-step workflows that may require revision.

Code generation stores intermediate values and composes several operations in one response, but shifts failures from schema misuse towards API, logic, and sandbox errors. H1 therefore relies on schema validation, while H2 requires execution feedback and bounded retry [7].

3.3Agent Architectures, State, and Domain Abstraction

H3 exposes higher-level domain operations inside the Python sandbox without adding a planner, working-memory module, or reflection controller. It tests how much task structure the interface should encode and how its values should support composition.

Planning and memory research describes relevant enterprise-task failures. ReAct shows the value of connecting reasoning, action, and observation in iterative tool use [31], although subsequent work has cautioned that these gains are not automatic and can depend heavily on prompting conditions. Indeed, Verma et al. [52] argue that ReAct’s performance on standard benchmarks is primarily attributable to exemplar–query similarity rather than the interleaved reasoning pattern itself. Planning surveys likewise show that task decomposition, refinement, and memory-augmented planning are active research areas, but they also underline that these mechanisms introduce additional control complexity [53]. This study doesn’t involve explicit planning, and instead asks whether a domain module can reduce burdens such as preserving identifiers, passing parameters, and choosing suitable operations.

State management is the closest point of contact with the memory literature. Enterprise architecture tasks often require carrying component identifiers, workspace references, report rows, and traversal results across operations. As mentioned, in H1, that state is mediated purely through the conversation history, while H2 and H3 can persist state inside the Python runtime. The memory literature distinguishes richer mechanisms such as episodic stores, vector retrieval, and structured long-term memory [54]; those are outside this thesis’s harness design. The relevant design question is how much useful intermediate state generated code can retain and how clearly domain-module return values expose it for subsequent operations.

Dependency-aware tool orchestration addresses a related problem: parameter flow across many tools. NaviAgent separates high-level task reasoning from low-level tool execution through a Tool World Navigation Model that encodes structural and behavioural dependencies between tools [55]. This thesis makes a simpler intervention. Rather than retrieving or precomputing a toolchain, H3 exposes reusable domain operations with signatures and return values shaped around common Ardoq workflows. For example, a traversal helper can return normalised node and edge structures with stable identifiers, while a report helper can bundle report discovery, filter validation, execution, and result formatting.

A developing line of work treats the agent-facing interface itself as the object of design rather than a wrapper over an existing surface. A recent systematisation frames such reusable, higher-level operations as a distinct “skills” layer sitting above atomic tools [56]. Pan [15] argues that CRUD APIs built for human interfaces are poorly suited to LLM planners and proposes an “agent-first” tool API with semantic verbs and normalised contracts, reporting higher task success than a CRUD baseline on the same platform and model. Mazrouei [16] shows that a domain-specific language designed for LLM generation can outperform general-purpose Python under an identical interpreter, especially on multi-step tasks. Chen et al. [57] hold the execution medium fixed and vary the abstraction level of agent-facing operations. They find that reusable higher-level skills cut token use substantially, while deep skill hierarchies degrade reliability. These results support the premise behind H3, that the abstraction level of the interface is a performance lever. A related line lets the agent author its own tools in code: CREATOR and CRAFT have the model synthesise and retrieve reusable functions on demand [58, 59]. H3 differs in that its abstractions are human-designed and fixed per platform, which makes them a controlled experimental variable rather than a moving, agent-generated target. The studies above therefore either remain at the tool-calling boundary, use agent-synthesised abstractions, or evaluate on generic benchmarks. None places the comparison inside a code-execution harness over a schema-governed enterprise platform.

Planning, reflection, and long-term memory remain adjacent rather than implemented mechanisms. H2 and H3 both use generated Python and sandbox state; H3 changes the operations and values available to that code.

3.4Enterprise AI and EA Automation

Enterprise architecture platforms are demanding for agent integration because they combine structured data, typed relationships, access control, and workflow semantics [17, 18]. In Ardoq, components are graph nodes with model-defined fields, references are directed typed edges, reports expose typed tabular results, and viewpoints encode reusable traversals. An agent must understand both the architectural meaning of components and the concrete metamodel of the workspace. Treating such a platform as a generic API surface risks failures that standard tool-use benchmarks do not capture [60].

Enterprise AI deployment also involves governance, auditability, and operational control, not only model accuracy [61]. EA platforms are relevant for harness design because they already encode governance over technology landscapes. Vendors have begun adding AI-assisted querying, reporting, and impact-analysis features [37, 62], but these products usually expose one interaction style rather than comparing alternative interfaces.

Recent enterprise-agent work addresses these constraints at several layers. Routine uses structured natural-language planning scripts with explicit steps, success criteria, and parameter-passing conventions; in one enterprise scenario it improved GPT-4o accuracy from 41.1% to 96.3% [63]. SkillForge shows that domain-contextualised skills grounded in tickets and technical documentation can outperform generic skills in cloud-support settings [64]. DADL tackles tool-library management with a declarative YAML format for serving many REST tools through one runtime, reducing tool-advertisement context cost by 142× in Code Mode [65]. Together, these studies support structure above the raw API.

Comparisons with established automation approaches reinforce the same point. Robotic Process Automation (RPA) remains faster and more reliable for stable repetitive workflows, while LLM agents require less development time and adapt more flexibly to changing interfaces [66]. POLARIS separates typed planning from governed execution through workflow contracts that specify allowed actions, data types, and transitions, reducing execution errors on back-office automation tasks [67]. These studies suggest that enterprise-agent reliability depends on the structure, governance, and recovery the harness provides.

Enterprise knowledge graph (EKG) research provides the closest conceptual parallel to Ardoq’s metamodel. EKGs represent organisational components, relationships, and metadata through formal schemas, and LLM agents benefit when this structure is explicit. Rolim, Freitas, and Vidal [41] show that metadata-grounded semantic views improve reasoning and traceability over enterprise knowledge graphs. The same issue appears in Ardoq: the agent must discover component types, fields, references, and workspace boundaries before acting. The harness determines whether this graph structure reaches the model as discrete tool schemas (H1), a typed client library (H2), or domain-level graph operations (H3).

Studies of MCP servers show that wrapping enterprise APIs into agent-facing tools is itself a design activity. Mastouri et al. [68] find that most MCP servers are REST-backed, that 92% expose tools as thin endpoint wrappers, and that the median server exposes only 19% of available REST operations. Multi-step workflows, administrative endpoints, and parameter-dense schemas are often omitted. This omission is technically consequential: exposing an entire REST API can create a large tool registry, consume context with dense schemas, increase security and governance risk, and present the agent with low-level operations whose safe use depends on state and procedural context not captured by the endpoint signature alone. Fault studies add that failures arise not only from the model but also from server configuration, tool registration, host communication, infrastructure settings, and documentation quality [69]. These findings support treating the harness as an interpretive layer between the platform and the model, not a neutral conduit.

The enterprise literature shows benefits from domain-specific planning, skills, tool libraries, and metadata grounding, but often varies several design choices at once, and does not provide a controlled within-platform harness comparison.

3.5Benchmark Design for Agent Evaluation

Agent evaluation has moved from static question answering toward executable environments where agents must interact with systems to complete tasks. This shift matters because performance depends on action space, environment state, task structure, and verification method as well as model capability. Benchmarks such as API-Bank, AgentBench, and WebArena show that tool-use performance is sensitive to environment design and available-tool composition [70, 71, 34].

Pysklo, Zhuravel, and Watson [20] characterise benchmark design through five axes: interaction model, environment, evaluation signal, observability, and task horizon. These choices determine what conclusions a benchmark can support. Trace matching gives detailed diagnostics but penalises valid alternative strategies; outcome or state verification better captures completion, but says less about the path taken. In contrast, this thesis adopts outcome-oriented verification because Ardoq tasks can often be completed through more than one valid sequence of operations. This requires tasks with answers that can be reliably derived from platform state, which excludes ambiguous tasks and open-ended subjective EA judgements.

Stateful evaluation exposes failures that stateless benchmarks miss. Lu et al. [45] argue that real tool use involves mutable world state, accumulated conversational context, and feedback loops; ToolSandbox evaluates intermediate and final milestones over arbitrary trajectories. Their results show that even strong models struggle with state dependencies, argument canonicalisation, and missing information. Jang et al. [72] similarly show that dispersed parameter information across dialogue turns significantly degrades tool-use performance. These findings matter for Ardoq because agents must preserve intermediate query results, component identifiers, and workspace context across multi-step workflows.

Trajectory-aware benchmarks add diagnostics beyond final success. ASTRA-bench decomposes difficulty into referential, functional, and informational complexity and shows that argument generation becomes a bottleneck under high complexity [19]. TRAJECT-Bench separately measures tool selection, argument correctness, and dependency satisfaction, exposing errors such as similar-tool confusion and parameter-blind selection [73]. REAP uses real developer-agent sessions and fail-to-pass tests, giving more realistic signals for model and harness selection [74]. These approaches were deemed beyond the scope of this thesis.

Reliability also requires repeated execution and perturbation. Yao and others [23] introduce pass[k], showing that pass@k can overstate production reliability. Agents with 60% single-run success may achieve only 25% consistency across five trials. Gupta [21] extends this into R(k,ϵ,λ), measuring consistency, robustness to equivalent prompt variations, and tolerance of infrastructure failures. Their results show substantial degradation under modest perturbation, making single-run ideal-condition evaluation insufficient for production-facing claims.

Enterprise and API-centric benchmarks are the most direct methodological precedents. Liu et al. [71] reports large performance variation across operating-system, database, and knowledge-graph environments, showing that aggregate scores hide domain-specific weaknesses. Pysklo, Zhuravel, and Watson [20] evaluate code-executing agents on sandboxed replicas of enterprise productivity APIs using state-diff contracts that compare initial and final environment state. The thesis follows this direction through a real enterprise platform, deterministic post-execution verification, and repeated trials per harness-task combination.

Existing benchmarks are valuable, but they are not designed to compare realised harness architectures within a single case-study enterprise architecture platform. The thesis benchmark is targeted: it compares the Traditional tool-calling (H1), the Programmatic (H2), and the Agent-native domain module (H3) harnesses in a realistic, curated EA environment.

3.6Summary and Gap

Prior work establishes that interface representation affects reliability, code adds state and control flow, and domain abstractions can reduce or displace coordination work [7, 8, 46, 47, 57]. Enterprise platforms add schema-governed data and workflows that generic benchmarks only partly capture [17, 18]. Their evaluation requires executable environments, objective verification, repeated trials, and trajectory diagnostics [20, 45, 72, 21].

However, the specific comparison remains open. Tool-specification studies usually stay within structured calling [7]; code studies use benchmarks without EA metamodels, enterprise contexts, and governed workflows [50]; and work on agent-first interfaces either remains at the tool boundary, uses agent-synthesised abstractions, or evaluates generic settings [15, 57, 16]. Enterprise frameworks also vary interface, planning, and recovery together [63, 64]. Thus, although the agent architecture space has been mapped [22], the trade-offs of the specific designs under study have not been measured within an enterprise EA platform.

This thesis addresses the gap through a controlled comparison on the Ardoq platform. H1–H2 is centred on invocation style and its consequences for state and observations; H2–H3 is centred on abstraction level over a shared execution model. The model, platform, tasks, and verification remain fixed, but each contrast compares a complete realised harness rather than an independently manipulated scalar property. The following chapters specify the method, implementation, and results.
chap:methodology:
This chapter outlines how the three harnesses were compared and how that comparison answers the research questions. It covers the experimental design, the benchmark suite and its validation, the harness configurations, the oracle-based verification, and the metrics and statistical tests used to interpret the results.

4.1Research Design and Comparisons

The study is a case study on a single platform, Ardoq. The three harnesses are compared on a shared task suite while everything except the harness itself is held fixed: the Ardoq deployment, model configuration, prompts, answer contracts, verifiers, and operational budgets are common to all three. Only their model-visible interfaces, documentation, state placement, and error mechanics differ, as the treatment under study.

The 24 fixed tasks are the paired unit of analysis. A cell combines one task with one harness, and a run is one of seven stochastic attempts within that cell. The seven runs per cell measure how stable each outcome is under non-determinism; the task remains the unit of analysis. The main campaign contains 72 task–harness cells and 504 total runs, as illustrated by Figure 4.1.

The two primary comparisons follow the sub-questions established in Chapter 1. SQ1 is the difference between H1 and H2 under the fixed benchmark and operational budgets, and SQ2 is the corresponding difference between H2 and H3. SQ3 examines how those differences vary across tasks and task characteristics. H1 and H3 are compared implicitly through the overall three-harness results, but they are not a planned contrast.

H1 exposes 20 low-level operations as JSON-schema tools. H2 makes the same operations available as Python functions through a single execute_code tool. H3 retains that execution model but replaces the low-level functions with an EA-oriented domain module. Table 4.1 summarises the three harnesses along the LLM-visible interface, invocation style, and comparison role.

Implementation testing showed two avoidable interface costs before the final campaign was run. H1’s raw tool observations could be large and repetitive, while H2’s source-style API documentation and typed return objects made the code-execution interface heavier than necessary. Because these choices would also matter for a production implementation, two small design-validation studies using A/B testing were run before fixing the final H1 and H2 configurations. Each study used T01–T05 with seven runs per variant. The purpose was not to test formatting or value representation as general causal factors, but to check whether a more compact implementation could reduce interaction cost without an observed loss in task completion on the subset. H1 and H2 each tested 2 variants, a and b. H1b and H2b were selected for the main harness comparison on that basis; subsequent references to H1 and H2 denote those canonical variants unless stated otherwise. H3 has only one configuration and was not A/B tested. Section 4.4 gives the scope and limits of these studies.

Table 4.2 links each sub-question to its comparison and evidence. Exact pass is the main correctness measure; resources and latency describe operational behaviour; traces and architecture-specific events support diagnosis. Interface representation can alter completion without changing the model [7, 8], so the harness is an experimental condition rather than a neutral implementation detail.

Failure analysis uses three evidence types: terminal outcomes, observed interaction events, and diagnostic interpretations from agent self-reflection or trace reading. A wrong answer without an execution fault does not identify its cause. Terminal outcomes are therefore primary, recorded mechanics are supporting evidence, and interpretations remain provisional.

4.2The Ardoq Benchmark Suite

The benchmark contains 24 analytical tasks selected from 142 candidates. It supports the harness comparison and is also a thesis contribution: no standard benchmark existed for Ardoq-centred agents. Each task translates a realistic EA workflow question into a repeatable, objectively verifiable case on the same local deployment. The complete task catalogue is provided in Appendix A.3.

The 24 tasks are numbered T01–T24 in a single sequence; the identifiers are labels and do not encode analytical categories. The analysis groups tasks by concept tags and by survey-rated difficulty rather than by any naming convention: the tags describe the retrieval pattern, computation pattern, and platform resources that the harnesses must handle, while difficulty captures practitioners’ perceived effort (detailed in Section 4.2.3).

4.2.1Task Construction

The benchmark was designed to include multi-step tasks with checkable answers. Work in enterprise architecture platforms spans tasks with widely varying levels of complexity. Simple direct retrieval tasks provide limited evidence about harness architecture because they require little coordination across operations. By contrast, open-ended questions such as whether an application should be retired depend on organisational context and professional judgement, and have no unique correct answer. The selected tasks target the middle ground between these extremes, covering multi-step workflows while remaining objectively answerable from platform state. These tasks reproduce analysis used before decisions, not the decisions themselves. This design enables controlled evaluation of realistic, multi-step analysis using deterministic oracle-based verification.

Task construction involved several steps, but started from Ardoq’s Solution Guides and their assets in the local seed environment. These packages configure reports, dashboards, viewpoints, workspaces, fields, types, relationships, and example data for recurring customer use cases. The resulting database is a multi-solution organisation rather than an isolated synthetic graph.

Before task candidate generation, a script queried the solutions included in the local environment and produced a summary for each one. A summary contained the solution description, its metamodel triples, and its bundled analytical assets. Candidate tasks were then created in two ways:

  • Manual exploration. The platform and its data were browsed directly, and questions were formulated from practical experience with Ardoq and an understanding of EA workflows.

  • Agentic exploration. Claude Code autonomously explored the environment using the solution summaries and four Python live-data probe utilities for reports, dashboards, viewpoints, and metamodel triples. It was also given the task criteria and a desired spread of task complexity, and drafted additional candidate questions, including compute functions.

The two methods produced 142 candidates covering topics such as application retirement, risk controls, capability coverage, and cost.

Each candidate used the same case fields. A case stores the task identifier, what field, why field, natural-language question, task-specific output type, tags, and verification function. The what field names the answer being requested, while the why field records the workflow reason the question matters. These fields are retained in the evaluation records and used in generated task tables, plots, and diagnostic summaries, so the benchmark preserves both the operational question and its EA motivation. The model must return structured output rather than free text, which makes exact comparison possible while preserving the possibility of multiple valid retrieval strategies. Listing 4.1 sketches the case structure for a representative task.

Selection of the approved tasks was entirely manual. Each candidate contract and oracle was executed, inspected, and refined or excluded when the oracle failed, returned an empty or unstable answer, required presentation logic that the agents could not access, or admitted several plausible interpretations. For example, some dashboard widgets apply filters to report data, and some viewpoints impose path requirements that are only available in the user interface. This manual testing and refinement was the most tedious part of task construction: it kept hard tasks while excluding ambiguous questions or cases whose expected answer was not stable and unambiguous in the live deployment.

Screening reduced 142 candidates to a target 24 tasks. All the retained tasks were tried with H1 and H2 during development. This helped identify ambiguous data, hidden filters, and presentation behaviour that the agents could not observe. Testing with H3 was avoided as much as possible, to avoid influencing the domain-module design based on task outcomes. However, early candidates were run with H3, to help with finding implementation bugs and ensuring matching functionality with H1/H2. Early runs with H3 did not result in adding task-specific domain operations, examples, or guardrails, however. The prompts, contracts, verifiers, task suite, and harnesses were then fixed for the final experiment campaign.

Selection was based on a common capability criterion. Every approved task has a reference solution expressible through the same 20 low-level tool operations shared by H1 and H2, without direct database access, private API shortcuts, or product UI affordances. This ensured there was a guaranteed agent-accessible solution, through the tool interface. H3 reaches the same task-relevant platform data through its domain module. This establishes that a valid low-level solution path exists; it does not imply that each harness can discover and execute that path within 45 turns and 90 seconds. The fixed budgets are part of the measured operating condition.

The tasks differ in the kinds of composition they require, using the dimensions from Section 2.4. Those five dimensions carry author-assigned ordinal scores (low, moderate, high) used only as descriptive structural proxies, not as independent experimental factors. Per-task difficulty is a separate construct: it is the practitioner rating from the validation survey (Section 4.2.3), on a one-to-five scale, rather than an author estimate.

Most tasks require at least two retrieval or analysis steps, such as discovering and reading a report, traversing from filtered components, joining retrieved sets, or aggregating values with field-specific null handling. T19 illustrates the low-coordination end: it reads two compact, named reports and performs a direct set difference, needing little schema discovery, fan-out, or intermediate state despite containing two retrievals.

The suite is read-only, which avoids state restoration but excludes conclusions about create, update, or delete operations.

4.2.2Task Taxonomy

Each task carries overlapping tags from a controlled vocabulary. Resource tags identify the platform resources the task requires: reports, dashboards, viewpoints, components, metamodel, or graph traversal. Computation tags describe operations such as aggregation, ranking, set operations, date filtering, hierarchy, and drill-down. Domain tags record the EA use case. Resource and computation tags support harness analysis, while domain tags ensure breadth across the Ardoq Solutions catalogue. The author-assigned tags are neither balanced factors nor statistically independent categories.

Table 4.3 gives a compact overview of the 24 approved tasks. It omits full prompts, ground-truth answers, and verifier logic; those details are reported in Appendix A.3.

4.2.3Task-suite Validation Survey

Because the benchmark is also a thesis deliverable, its tasks were reviewed for realism independently of the harness comparison. Seven respondents, all software developers at Ardoq, one of them the author’s supervisor, were asked to take an enterprise-architect perspective and rate each of the 24 tasks on three five-point dimensions: difficulty (how hard the task would be to carry out), usefulness (how relevant its answer is to EA work), and frequency (how often such a question arises in practice). The instrument shown to respondents is reproduced in Appendix A.9. No identifying information is retained; only the aggregate role summary and per-task mean and median ratings are reported.

The respondents are platform-internal rather than independent external EA practitioners, and the sample is small, so the survey gives indicative rather than confirmatory validation (more details in Section 4.8). Its principal use in the analysis is the difficulty dimension: the per-task survey mean is the difficulty score used throughout the task-sensitivity analysis. The survey results are reported alongside the rest of the empirical findings in Chapter 6.

4.2.4Oracle-Based Verification

Each task module recomputes the expected answer from the live Ardoq API at verification time. The verifier compares this result with the typed agent output without inspecting its reasoning or requiring a particular trace.

Exact equality is defined per output type rather than as raw object identity. Name and identifier collections are compared as unordered sets, so a correct answer is independent of output ordering unless the task explicitly requires a ranking with a stated tie-break. Numeric answers are avoided where a discrete count, set, or boolean suffices. Where an average or rate is intrinsic to the question, for example the cost averages of T08 and T24 or the compliance rate of T14, the expected and actual values are rounded to the task-specified precision and compared within a fixed tolerance. Each task fixes its own comparison rule in its verifier; the per-task rules are documented in Appendix A.3.

The oracle is independent of the agent trace, but not of the shared client code.
