It is separate from the agent run and uses the same function definitions that generate the H1 tools, plus ordinary Python for deterministic post-processing. It has no direct database access, unrestricted API, or shortcut unavailable to the harnesses. A computable oracle therefore establishes a valid low-level solution path; the comparison tests whether agents can discover and compose it.

Each oracle was validated during task construction by executing its compute function against the live instance and manually checking that it produced one stable, interpretable answer before approval. The dated answer snapshots in Appendix A.3 record those checks rather than experimental outcomes. At verification time, the oracle re-executes its canonical query path and never reuses or observes the agent’s trace. However, it shares low-level client functions with H1 and H2.

This avoids brittle trace matching and subjective LLM-as-a-judge scoring, but it does not measure procedural quality. Traces and generated code are retained and occasionally inspected and analysed manually, because outcome-only evaluation can sometimes mask questionable successful procedures [75].

Where an output can be flattened into comparable answer elements, the verifier also records precision, recall, F1 score, extra-item count, and missing-item count. These measures diagnose over-retrieval and under-retrieval but do not replace the task-specific exact-pass rule. They are not treated as equally meaningful for scalar, Boolean, ranked, and nested structured outputs.

4.3Architecture Configurations

All harnesses use the exact same frontier model through the same Ardoq-internal LiteLLM proxy route. Claude Sonnet 4.6 (model identifier claude-sonnet-4-6) was chosen, due to its balance between cost efficiency and frontier-level intelligence. The runner supplies neither temperature nor seed, leaving the provider default temperature of 1.0, to mirror the production environment. Seven repetitions per cell provide a cost-bounded view of sampling variability.

Table 4.4 records the common configuration. Prompts share a controlled skeleton, while interface-specific instructions and documentation remain part of each condition. Runs were recorded on 15 and 16 June 2026 against the same seeded deployment.

The seed snapshot was pulled on 3 June 2026. The implementation, benchmark source, result archives, and database snapshot are internal and are not published with the thesis.

One turn is one model request, whether the model returns an answer or requests one or more actions. The 45-turn and 90-second limits were chosen during development to bound campaign time and cost. Informal development runs indicated that attempts still unresolved near these limits rarely recovered, although this observation was not recorded as a formal pilot study, but chosen based on engineering judgement. Turn-limit and timeout outcomes are therefore reported separately from wrong answers. A timeout is checked only after the current model or tool node has completed and before another model request begins; it does not interrupt an in-flight call. Consequently, elapsed time can exceed 90 seconds, but each retained tool request has a corresponding return value.

The model route used its default five-minute prompt cache. Cache reads were disabled on the first turn of each run, while cache writes remained enabled. This prevents later repetitions from receiving a pre-heated cache from earlier runs and gives each harness the same first-turn baseline. Later requests within the same run could reuse eligible prefixes established by that run.

4.3.1Traditional Tool-Calling Harness Configuration

H1 exposes low-level Ardoq platform operations as JSON-schema tools registered with the agent framework. The catalogue contains 20 tools across component, entity-resolution, traversal, report, metamodel, viewpoint, and dashboard domains, all of which are registered for every task. The model emits one or more structured calls, the framework validates and dispatches them, and the serialised results become observations in the conversation history.

4.3.2Programmatic Harness Configuration

H2 exposes the same underlying operation set as pre-bound async Python functions inside a Docker-hosted sandbox. The LLM-visible interface contains a single tool, execute_code. Its description includes generated Python documentation for the full API. Variables and imports persist across code executions within one task run, allowing the model to retain intermediate identifiers and results. A fresh sandbox session identifier is created for every run.

4.3.3Domain-Module Harness Configuration

H3 uses the same sandbox and execute_code interaction model as H2, but changes the pre-imported namespace. Instead of Python functions, it exposes an EA-oriented domain module with declarative query predicates, typed domain models, metamodel inspection, report-analysis helpers, and a chainable traversal builder. H3 therefore varies abstraction level without adding an external planner, memory store, or separate orchestration controller.

4.3.4Prompt and Documentation Protocol

All harnesses share the same role framing, answer procedure, and instruction to return either the typed output or an explicit failure. H1 then describes its tools, while H2 and H3 describe persistent Python environments using raw-API and domain-module idioms. The shared prompt text was written once, and the three prompts appear in Appendix A.5. H1 carries 20 JSON schemas; H2 and H3 embed their complete references in execute_code. No condition receives task-specific hints or a preselected subset of operations: every task sees the full, task-invariant interface of its harness, and the agent must identify the appropriate resources and actions itself. These unfiltered definitions also create a fixed per-harness context cost that is measured separately.

4.4Harness-Configuration Design-Validation Studies

Two design-validation studies, each structured as an A/B comparison, fixed how H1 serialised results and how H2 documented its API and represented values. They select conditions for the main comparison rather than test the research questions independently. Each study used the first five approved tasks, T01–T05, with seven runs per task and variant. The first five tasks were selected for convenience rather than sampled to represent the full benchmark, but they were manually checked to provide an informative configuration check. Table 4.5 summarises the variants, and Section 6.2 reports the observed outcomes. The B versions were selected for the main comparison, and referred to as the canonical variants.

4.4.1H1: How Should Tool Results Be Returned?

H1a serialises each tool result as the raw structured object the API returns, including null fields. This matches how Ardoq’s production agents currently return tool results, so it is the incumbent baseline. H1b instead returns results through compact, type-specific string encodings: null and empty fields are omitted where they add no task-visible information, and row-oriented outputs from reports and dashboards use pipe-delimited tables. The two variants register identical tool schemas and dispatch identical calls; they differ only in how the result of each call is written back into the conversation. Because H1 re-sends the full conversation on every turn (Section 2.5), result serialisation drives context growth directly. The study therefore reports total token usage and final context size alongside the pass rate. The question, framed against the production baseline, is whether H1b’s more efficient encoding is a safe improvement over the current approach or whether dropping nulls and flattening tables removes information the model relies on.

4.4.2H2: How Should the Code Environment Expose the API?

H2a documents the available operations by emitting their full Python class source used in the Pydantic tool definitions, through inspect.getsource. It has the bound sandbox functions return typed Pydantic objects, the most faithful rendering of the underlying API and the naive starting point for a code-execution interface. H2b documents the same operations as inline dictionary schemas and has the functions return plain dictionaries and ordinary Python data structures. The variants use the same low-level operations and sandbox, but two properties changed together: documentation form and returned Python value type. Their individual effects cannot be separated. The motivating hypothesis was that full class definitions add context without improving operation use, and that ordinary dictionaries are sufficient for generated code. The study records pass rate, tool-definition size, final context, tokens, and cost. The compact variants selected from these limited checks are H1b and H2b; where the suffix is immaterial, the thesis refers to them as H1 and H2.

4.5Experimental Procedure

The runner loads tasks, constructs the cases, and starts one worker per harness. Workers share the model gateway and Ardoq deployment, while tasks and repetitions run sequentially within each worker. Tasks ran in a fixed order, with the seven repetitions for each task adjacent.

For each task and repetition, the runner creates a fresh logical sandbox session where applicable and drives the agent’s model–tool loop. H2 and H3 do not start a new Docker container per run; instead, a persistent FastAPI sandbox container allocates a new session namespace keyed by a fresh identifier. Variables and imports persist within that run’s namespace, but not across runs. The run terminates when the agent returns a structured result, exceeds the turn budget, reaches the timeout boundary, or encounters an unhandled error.

On normal completion, the task verifier recomputes the oracle answer and compares it with the model output. The run is classified as pass, wrong answer, explicit failure ("giving up"), turn-limit exhaustion, timeout, or unexpected error. A wrong answer, turn-limit result, or timeout triggers one separate reflection call with the same model and a typed failure schema. The reflection sees the task and run history, including pending tool returns at a timeout boundary, and the oracle answer. It selects from the fixed categories reproduced in Appendix A.7 and gives a short reason. All 131 eligible non-passing runs in the main campaign produced a reflection record. Reflection is agent self-report, does not change the terminal outcome, and is excluded from the run’s model-usage totals. An explicit failure already contains the agent’s stated category and therefore does not trigger a second call.

The wall-clock timer starts when the per-run function is entered, after case construction. The recorded total includes model gateway transit, model requests, tool execution, sandbox work for H2 and H3, orchestration, and oracle verification. It excludes Docker startup, offline task loading, and reflection.

Each completed run is stored with its configuration, messages, tool schemas, outputs, oracle verdict, usage, latency, terminal outcome, and reflection. This permits campaign batches to be merged and audited without reconstructing the interaction from aggregate tables.

4.6Evaluation Metrics

The analysis distinguishes headline outcomes from supporting and architecture-specific diagnostics.

Headline outcomes.

Exact pass is the primary correctness measure. A run passes only when its typed output satisfies the task-specific verifier. Total model tokens, estimated cost, and recorded end-to-end latency measure the operational burden under the fixed budgets. All runs, including wrong answers and budget-bound outcomes, enter these operational summaries.

Supporting behavioural measures.

These include turns, final context size, LLM-visible actions, model and tool latency components, terminal outcome counts, and applicable collection precision, recall, and F1. Final context size is the input-token count of the final model request. An LLM-visible action is one H1 tool call or one H2/H3 execute_code call. It is not a platform-operation count: one code action may perform several Ardoq calls.

Provider usage metadata records base input, cache reads and writes, and output tokens for every request. Total tokens include all reported input categories and output. “New input” is recorded input minus cache-read tokens, so it retains base input and cache-write tokens. Per-run cost applies the June 2026 price schedule for the model route separately to base input, cache reads, cache writes, and output. The reported cost is therefore cache-adjusted rather than a flat list-price calculation. Because first-turn cache reads are disabled, the measured cache-read tokens provide an even comparison across runs, because it avoids the reuse of a pre-warmed cache by an earlier repetition.

Architecture-specific diagnostics.

H1 records malformed tool calls and framework retries. H2 and H3 record sandbox syntax, runtime, and API events plus generated code lines; a code line is a non-empty, non-comment source line. H2 also logs calls made to its low-level functions inside the sandbox. H3 composes platform work inside domain operations and does not expose equivalent inner-call telemetry. Inner-call counts are therefore not compared across all three harnesses, only H1 and H2. These diagnostics help explain a result but are not interchangeable measures of interface complexity.

4.7Analysis Plan

The analysis begins with run counts, means, distributions, and task-level patterns. Inferential tests use the task as the unit of pairing. For each harness, the seven runs in a task are first aggregated to a task mean. The 24 paired task means then enter a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test for exact pass rate, cost, total tokens, all-run wall-clock latency, model latency, tool latency, and turns. The primary comparisons are H1 versus H2 for SQ1 and H2 versus H3 for SQ2; H1 versus H3 is secondary. All-run resource and latency values enter these tests, so budget-bound outcomes remain part of the operating-cost comparison.

Zero paired differences are discarded using Wilcoxon’s zero method, absolute differences receive average ranks when tied, and the implementation chooses the exact or asymptotic calculation supported by the observed ties and zeros. Results report the test statistic, median paired difference, and rank-biserial correlation. The tests are implemented with SciPy and statsmodels in the generated analysis pipeline. With only 24 paired tasks and coarse pass rates based on seven runs, the tests support rather than replace the task-level evidence.

Exact pass is the primary metric for testing whether the harnesses differ; the tests of tokens, cost, latency, and turns provide supporting evidence. Holm’s correction is applied separately for each metric. For exact pass, it adjusts the H1–H2 and H2–H3 p-values together; total token use has its own pair, and the same approach is used for each remaining metric. The correction therefore does not treat every metric and comparison as one large family.

Terminal outcomes and internal error events are reported descriptively as counts and proportions. No inferential claim is based on the agent’s reflection categories. Collection precision, recall, F1, and extra- and missing-item counts are also descriptive because their interpretation depends on output structure and they are unavailable or less meaningful for some tasks. The failure analysis reports these measures on non-passing eligible runs so that successful exact matches do not inflate the diagnosis of partial answers.

SQ3 remains exploratory. Per-tag correctness and resource use are reported with task counts, recognising that tags overlap and are unbalanced. Spearman rank correlations relate the survey-derived difficulty score (per-task mean rating, 1–5) to per-task mean pass rate, cost, tokens, turns, and latency for each harness. These tests are not corrected for multiplicity and are interpreted as descriptive evidence of monotonic association, not as causal difficulty effects, due to the low volume of tasks and iterations.

Practical quantities lead the interpretation: percentage-point pass differences, additional completed runs, paired task patterns, token differences, and cost per run.

4.8Validity and Limitations

4.8.1Internal Validity

The staged contrasts hold the benchmark, model, platform, output contracts, verification, caching, and budgets constant, but each harness is a package of related design choices. H1 versus H2 changes action representation together with state placement, documentation, observation flow, and error handling. H2 versus H3 changes domain operations, return structures, hidden composition, and observability. Prompt and documentation differences are constitutive parts of those treatments. The study therefore estimates differences between the three implemented conditions, not pure effects of invocation style or abstraction in all possible implementations.

Harness workers also share a model gateway and Ardoq deployment. Concurrent scheduling and transient service load may affect latency unevenly, even though the same scheduling policy applies to each condition. The fixed turn and time budgets can interact differently with the architectures; this is intended when measuring bounded completion, but it does not estimate unconstrained capability. Development involved manual inspection of tasks, oracles, prompts, and traces, and all three harnesses were exercised during construction. The scored results did not change the tasks or harnesses, but the author developed the benchmark and the harnesses in the same project. Task realism, usefulness, and difficulty were rated in the validation survey, but the seven respondents are platform-internal developers, one the author’s supervisor, rather than independent external EA practitioners, so this is indicative rather than independent review. Direct lookup tasks are underrepresented, and development runs informed the retained task definitions. The resulting suite may favour compositional cases on which harness differences are easier to observe. The design-validation subset was selected by convenience, and its selected H1b/H2b runs are reused in the main totals.

4.8.2Construct Validity

Exact pass measures agreement with a deterministic answer contract, not explanation quality or procedural appropriateness. Tokens and cost measure model interaction burden rather than total compute or intrinsic algorithmic efficiency. LLM-visible actions are not comparable platform-operation counts, generated code lines are a rough diagnostic, and agent reflections are self-reports. The difficulty score is a survey mean from seven internal respondents and is treated as a coarse continuous summary, while tags overlap and are not balanced factors. Collection metrics and retained traces add context, but they do not eliminate these gaps between measures and constructs.

4.8.3Statistical Conclusion Validity

The study has 24 paired tasks and seven stochastic runs per cell. This supports paired task-level comparison but gives coarse per-task pass rates and limited power for small differences. Runs within a task do not provide independent evidence of task breadth. Ties and zero differences between harnesses reduce the effective sample for signed-rank tests, subgroup cells can contain only one or two tasks, and latency and token distributions are skewed. Difficulty and tag analyses are therefore exploratory, and descriptive effect sizes remain central.

4.8.4External Validity and Scope

The comparison uses one model route, one seeded Ardoq deployment, and one implementation of each harness. The seed contains Solution Guide assets and fictional demonstration data rather than live customer records. It is structurally rich but cannot reproduce production drift, organisation-specific modelling, or every Ardoq installation. Other models and EA platforms may respond differently to schemas, code, and domain documentation. In particular, the H3 result applies to this module’s names, operation boundaries, validation rules, and assumptions, not to all agent-native interfaces.

The 24 tasks cover analytical workflows. They do not test mutation, approval workflows, concurrent users, external integrations, or long-running operations. Security is also a deliberate scope exclusion. The experimental sandbox and domain module are research implementations, not claims of production hardening. A production deployment would need separate analysis of isolation, permissions, auditability, data leakage, resource limits, and safe write operations.

4.8.5Measurement and Oracle Validity

The oracle is independent of the agent trace but shares low-level client code with H1 and H2, so a common client or interpretation error could affect both execution and verification. Manual answer checks reduce but cannot remove this risk. Total latency includes oracle verification without a separate verifier timer, and inner platform calls are not observed equivalently in H3. Latency attribution therefore relies on the model and tool components, while cross-harness conclusions use only measurements available under comparable boundaries.
