This chapter explains how the experimental conditions were built, focusing on what the model can discover, invoke, retain, observe, and repair.

5.1Implementation goals and architecture

The implementation builds three harnesses that interact with one Ardoq deployment. H1 presents twenty low-level operations as individual tools. H2 exposes the same operations as asynchronous Python functions through execute_code. H3 retains that execution environment but replaces the functions with an agent-native domain module.

Figure 5.1 shows the runtime paths. All conditions use the same evaluation runner, model route, typed answer contract, and authentication-bound API client layer. H2 and H3 also use the same Docker-hosted executor. Sharing the executor rules out its Python version, container configuration, session policy, and startup behaviour as sources of H2-to-H3 difference. The remaining H2–H3 differences are namespace, documentation, returned structures, guard rails, and work hidden inside H3 operations.

Table 5.1 separates shared parts from harness-specific parts using the harness responsibilities and state locations defined in Chapter 2.

5.2Common experimental foundation

5.2.1Agent and answer contract

All three agents use pydantic-ai and the same Claude Sonnet 4.6 deployment. The framework assembles history, registers tools, records usage, applies prompt caching, and validates the final Pydantic output.

For a given task, every harness receives the same natural-language question and must return the same task-specific success type or a common explicit failure type. A success object may contain, for example, a list of server records or a mapping from capabilities to organisational units. The explicit failure object contains a categorical cause and a short explanation. The agent returns it as its final structured output; it is not an exception. Malformed structured output instead activates the framework’s output-validation retry. This differs from H2 or H3 code exception handling: a Python traceback is returned as an ordinary tool observation, after which the model may choose to submit another snippet.

The oracle is not part of the agent contract. The evaluation runner invokes it after the agent terminates, as described under oracle-based verification in Chapter 4. Consequently, the harness cannot use the oracle result while constructing its answer.

5.2.2Shared low-level operations and their production origin

H1 and H2 share one ordered catalogue of twenty logical operations. The catalogue extends the seventeen production tools described in Table 2.3. Three operations were added for the benchmark: get_component_aggregations computes values and filter_components filters and applies field-level conditions within a type, while list_component_types enumerates valid types. These additions extend the existing client and backend.

Table 5.2 gives the complete operation set. The same ordered list is the source of truth for H1 registration and H2 namespace construction. H3 has different operation boundaries, although it reaches the task-relevant data through the same deployment and client API handlers.

Authentication and communication logic is hidden from the model. The framework or namespace wrapper injects the deployment URL, API key, and organisation label. The function then calls an authentication-bound client handler, which issues the corresponding REST request. This keeps credentials outside model-generated arguments and gives H1 and H2 a common lower layer.

5.2.3Evaluation cases, runs, and persistence

An evaluation case binds a task specification to one harness. At the start of each repetition, the runner creates a run record and installs harness-specific dependencies, including a fresh H2/H3 session identifier.

The runner records requests, messages, schemas, timing, usage, actions, generated code, and observable errors. After termination, it adds the output, oracle verdict, terminal outcome, and any eligible reflection. A serialisable snapshot omits credentials and live callables but retains the task code and configuration.

Before a campaign, the runner creates a JSON result file and then replaces it atomically after each run under an asynchronous write lock. This preserves completed work during interruption. Snapshots support later merging, and merged results retain their source provenance.

5.3From implementation artifacts to model-visible interfaces

Each interface has three parts: an executable function, wrapper, or SDK class; a generated schema or reference; and the format returned to the model (as illustrated in Figure 5.2).

For H1, pydantic-ai converts each low-level function’s signature and docstring into a JSON tool definition. Its parameter schema omits the injected connection context. Returned Pydantic objects then pass through the selected H1 serialiser before entering conversation history.

For H2, a namespace factory wraps each low-level function as a credential-bound asynchronous callable. A documentation generator renders the callable’s Python signature and referenced Pydantic models and enumerations. One execute_code schema carries the complete API reference.

H3 starts from a separately designed domain module over the common client handlers. Its namespace factory inserts public classes and constructors under known names. An abstract-syntax-tree generator emits class stubs with signatures and docstrings while replacing method bodies with ellipses. Curated examples are prepended to that reference. Generated code therefore executes against a pre-populated namespace; it does not import either the H2 functions or H3 SDK.

Table 5.3 reports the frozen interface sizes, measured with LiteLLM’s token counter for the evaluated model route. These are sizes before any task run begins, not complete-run usage. The serialisation and documentation variants summarised in its final column are defined in Sections 5.4.2 and 5.6.2.

5.4H1: Traditional tool-calling harness

5.4.1Runtime path and state placement

H1 supplies all twenty low-level schemas with each model request. The framework validates selected calls, injects connection context, invokes the functions, and appends their serialised results to the history. The agentic loop ends with a typed success or failure, after which the runner performs oracle verification and, for eligible non-passing outcomes, a separate reflection call. A request may contain several independent calls, but any later call that needs an identifier, field name, or relationship discovered in an earlier observation requires another model request.

Retrieved identifiers and records are stored only in conversation history because H1 has no task-visible execution state. The model must recover them from observations for dependent calls. Every domain operation is therefore traceable in the history, although internal reasoning is not.

5.4.2Observation serialisation variants

H1a and H1b expose identical tool names, descriptions, and parameter schemas. They differ only in observation encoding. H1a returns the default serialisation of the Pydantic result, including nested structure and null fields. H1b removes null fields and whitespace from JSON. Search and entity-resolution outputs use a pipe-delimited table where the result consists mainly of rows. H1a is the existing production behaviour, while H1b is the proposed compact alternative.

Compact serialisation reduces observation volume without changing operation coverage, but it can affect how the model interprets absent or nested values. It is an empirically checked encoding choice, not a cognitively equivalent one. Listing 5.1 and Listing 5.2 show the two observation shapes for the same report lookup.

The H1 variants differ only in how tool observations are written back into the conversation. The following excerpt shows the same kind of report lookup in the reference encoding and in the compact encoding used for the main comparison.

5.5Shared Python execution service

H2 and H3 send generated source, a namespace mode, and a session identifier through execute_code to a persistent Docker-hosted FastAPI service. The service:

  1. selects or creates the namespace associated with the session;

  2. compiles the source with Python’s top-level-await flag;

  3. executes it against pre-bound H2 functions or H3 SDK objects;

  4. captures output streams, exceptions, and available inner-call records;

  5. returns a formatted observation to the agent; and

  6. retains the namespace for a later action in the same run.

Figure 5.3(a) shows the treatment-specific runtime loop for the traditional tool-calling harness (H1). Figure 5.3(b) shows the corresponding path for the programmatic harnesses (H2/H3). The evaluation loop sends generated Python to the Docker-hosted service, whose namespace mode selects H2’s Ardoq functions or H3’s domain module. In both panels, the agent run is followed by the same oracle verification and optional reflection procedure.

5.5.1Session namespaces and concurrency

Each H2/H3 run receives a fresh UUID whose namespace stores variables, imports, and functions across code actions. Values created before an exception remain under normal Python semantics. Namespaces persist until the container stops, but fresh unguessable identifiers prevent later campaign runs from selecting earlier state.

Harness campaigns may run concurrently, while cases within one harness proceed sequentially. Per-request output capture uses ContextVar-backed stream wrappers. This prevents concurrent asyncio tasks from writing into one another’s stdout or stderr buffer. The evaluation protocol submits one code action at a time for a given agent run, so no two snippets intentionally mutate the same session namespace concurrently.

A snippet can retain thousands of identifiers or rows while printing only a count, sample, or final projection. Printed content becomes conversation state; unprinted values remain in execution state until inspected.

5.5.2Observations, errors, and limits

The service returns captured output, a structured execution error, and available platform-call records as labelled observation sections. Normalised success and error fields support later classification without creating another model action.

The client applies a 30-second timeout to each executor request. The formatted model observation is capped at 50,000 characters after execution. This cap limits what enters conversation state but does not truncate Python objects already retained in the session namespace. The system prompt therefore tells the model to print summaries and required answer fields rather than entire catalogues. Table 5.4 collects the behaviourally relevant properties of the execution service.

The service is a sandbox for this read-only experiment, not a hardened production sandbox. Production use would require threat-model-specific controls for credentials, isolation, network access, resources, session disposal, and auditing (Section 2.5).

5.6H2: Programmatic harness

5.6.1Wrapped-function namespace

Beyond the wrapped callables described in Section 5.3, the H2 namespace also exposes json. Each wrapper records its function name, arguments, elapsed time, and error flag, so one model-visible execute_code action can contain several low-level calls, including calls launched together with asyncio.gather. The runner stores these inner records separately from the single model-visible action. This distinction is necessary later: an LLM tool-call count measures submitted snippets for H2, while the inner log measures wrapped low-level operations.

5.6.2Documentation and value variants

The code-execution tool description explains session persistence, top-level await, explicit printing, and the observation cap. It then includes a generated reference for all twenty functions.

H2a renders each signature and performs a breadth-first walk over referenced Pydantic models and enumerations. The Python source of the classes in the tool signatures is included with inspect.getsource. Those same classes are injected into the sandbox runtime for the agent to use. H2b instead expands each model into a compact dictionary schema, renders enum members as literal unions, merges model unions into nullable fields, and bounds recursive expansion at three levels. The excerpt in Listing 5.3 and Listing 5.4 shows the difference. H2a is the baseline implementation: expose the Python source and preserve the typed objects returned by the underlying functions. H2b deliberately translates both layers into simpler structures for model-generated code: the documentation becomes inline dictionary schemas, and return values are recursively converted from Pydantic models to dictionaries and from enumerations to primitive values, so generated code uses key access rather than Pydantic attribute access.

The H2 variants make the same raw Ardoq operations available through execute_code, but render their documentation differently. H2a exposes source-like function and model definitions; H2b keeps the same call contract but compresses the return shape into an inline dictionary schema.

The H2 design-validation study changes two linked properties: H2a documents and returns Pydantic objects, while H2b uses inline dictionary documentation and returns dictionaries. Both expose the same logical low-level operation coverage. H2b is the canonical condition selected by the process in Section 4.4.

5.7H3: Agent-native domain module harness

H3 implements the agent-native definition from Section 2.6; it is not a universal template. Six principles guided its public interface:

  1. use enterprise-architecture vocabulary rather than endpoint-shaped names;

  2. make query and traversal operations composable and declarative in Python;

  3. normalise platform responses into stable domain objects;

  4. move recurring discovery, batching, hydration, and graph coordination into reusable code;

  5. reject bounded classes of invalid or unbounded actions with diagnostic errors; and

  6. generate the reference from current signatures and docstrings.

5.7.1Design rationale and programming model

The SDK is declarative for selecting components and describing graph traversals. A Q expression records type, name, workspace, or field predicates; ComponentQuery.fetch() materialises the selection; and TraversalBuilder accumulates hops until build() executes them. The SDK selects the lower-level calls, batching, and hydration, while hiding implementation details from the agent.

This is bounded declarative programming, not a general query optimiser. Construction is local; fetch() and build() are explicit asynchronous execution points; and each traversal hop still requires platform work. The design changes who coordinates that work. Table 5.5 summarises these programming stages.

Returned domain objects, rather than API calls, are H3’s main values passed between operations. Query results directly seed traversal or viewpoint execution, and the resulting Subgraph supports filtering, aggregation, and further queries. Listing 5.5 shows this value flow. Generated code does not need to extract identifiers into a second request structure or join reference endpoints back to separately fetched records.

The same predicate vocabulary applies to component queries, report rows, and subgraph filters. Arguments are generally flexible to accept Python callables, components, identifiers, or derived ID sets, so H3 constrains common operations without replacing task-specific Python with a fixed workflow engine.

The interface separates awaited retrieval methods such as fetch() and build() from synchronous analysis over materialised values. Frozen dataclasses and non-mutating filters make session state predictable and allow repeated analysis without another fetch, as demonstrated in Listing 5.6.

Normalisation reduces the code needed to reshape returned data as well as orchestration. Components expose stable identity and fields, references resolve their endpoints, reports carry metadata and rows, and subgraphs remove dangling relationships. H3 is therefore more than a renaming of H2’s functions.

5.7.2Public namespace and model-facing guidance

Table 5.6 lists the eighteen pre-populated names in the H3 namespace. Snippets require no imports, removing module-path and symbol resolution errors observed during development.

The execute_code description combines runtime rules, six hand-written composition patterns, and a generated SDK reference. The doc generation uses Python’s ast module to remove private members and method bodies while preserving public signatures, types, properties, and docstrings in ordered sections. This keeps the structural reference aligned with the source. The composition patterns remain manual and are reproduced with extended examples in Appendix A.6.

5.7.3Moving work into the SDK

The SDK moves parts of the five burdens from Section 2.4 between generated and reusable code (Table 5.7). The main change is that retrieved objects can be reused directly in traversal and local analysis.

For example, a component query resolves types, retrieves identifiers, batches hydration, and returns objects that can form a traversal frontier. The builder retains a normalised subgraph across hops, while report and subgraph analysis runs locally over retrieved data. Table 5.8 gives representative model-visible operations alongside the coordination they hide.

5.7.4Guard rails and diagnostic feedback

Q.name(), Q.type(), and Q.workspace() reject regular expressions without literal alphabetic characters, preventing wildcard-only catalogue retrieval.

TraversalBuilder validates sufficiently specified hops against the metamodel and reports valid relationships after a mismatch. It checks schema compatibility, not whether the path answers the task. Frontiers above 200 components similarly raise a diagnostic that requests narrower filters. Listing 5.7 shows a representative traversal configuration and subsequent local analysis.

5.8Example workflow across the three harnesses

T02 asks for servers supporting applications scheduled to retire within twelve months with no named successor, together with each server’s hosting type and lifecycle phase. It exercises schema discovery, date filtering, successor checking, graph traversal, and enrichment. Table 5.9 summarises the first run of each harness from the main campaign. The table omits returned rows but preserves the operations and state transitions.

The stages are comparable, but their boundaries differ. H1 carries parameters between model turns; H2 keeps them in Python while retaining low-level operations; H3 carries state in compatible domain objects while the module handles recurring retrieval mechanics. Chapter 6 tests the consequences.

5.9Telemetry, validation, and measurement boundaries

The evaluation records telemetry at six boundaries: provider responses, runner timers, model-visible message history, executor logs, agent termination, and oracle verification. These boundaries matter because the three harnesses expose different amounts of internal work. A count taken at the conversation boundary is available for all harnesses, but it does not measure the same kind of work as an HTTP-call log inside H2. The analysis therefore treats run-level usage, latency, outcome, and model-visible actions as cross-harness measures, while inner-call records and reflection records are diagnostic evidence. Table 5.10 records the capture points; Section 4.6 defines their aggregation.

The latency split follows the same boundary. Provider timestamps separate model time from model-visible tool time. H2 and H3 executor work is included in tool time because both enter the sandbox through execute_code. H2 then adds wrapper-level timings for each low-level function called inside the snippet. H3 does not expose an equivalent inner log: SDK methods may combine validation, hydration, batching, traversal, and several REST requests under one domain operation. A flat internal call count would not have the same meaning as the H2 wrapper log, so it is not used as a cross-harness metric.

End-to-end run latency starts when the runner enters a case and ends after oracle verification. It includes model requests, model-visible tool execution, sandbox work, orchestration overhead, and verifier execution. It excludes Docker startup, offline task loading, post-run reflection, and figure generation.

Validation also occurs at several boundaries. Before a run, a health endpoint checks that the backend is reachable. During a run, framework schemas, executor exceptions, API errors, and H3 domain checks return structured feedback to the agent. After termination, the task oracle computes the expected answer and compares it with the final typed output. These checks support benchmark validity, not general software assurance.

This measurement contract supports the two comparisons from Methodology: tool calling versus code over the same low-level operations, and low-level functions versus an agent-native domain module in the same executor. Chapter 6 evaluates the resulting correctness, resource use, latency, and failure patterns.
chap:evaluation:
This chapter compares the three harnesses, locates their task-level differences, and interprets the results for agent–system interface design. Measurements are kept separate from proposed mechanisms.

6.1Overview

The main campaign contains seven runs in each of 72 task–harness cells: 168 runs per harness and 504 total. H1 and H2 denote the canonical H1b and H2b variants selected in Section 6.2.

SQ1 compares tool calling with programmatic composition over the same low-level coverage; SQ2 compares low-level Python functions with the agent-native domain module; and SQ3 locates their task sensitivity. Exact pass is the primary outcome. Resources, terminal outcomes, and telemetry support interpretation.

H2 passes far more often than H1 and uses fewer model resources, especially for graph, set, cross-source, and state-heavy workflows. H3 reduces token traffic and final context relative to H2 while giving up only one exact answer; per-run model cost also falls from $0.11 to $0.10, while mean latency changes only descriptively from 34.8s to 30.8s. The H2–H3 step is therefore mainly a gain in interaction efficiency, with little change in correctness.

6.1.1Task-suite Validation

Before interpreting harness behaviour, the suite itself was checked for realism through the validation survey described in Section 4.2.3. Table 6.1 pools the seven respondents’ ratings across the 24 tasks. Usefulness is the strongest signal, at a mean of 3.70 out of 5 (median 4); most tasks have a median usefulness of 4 or higher, so the questions map onto answers the respondents regard as relevant to EA work. Frequency is lower at 2.57 (median 2), consistent with periodic analytical or deep-dive questions rather than daily lookups. Rated difficulty averages 2.99 and ranges from 1.71 to 4.00 across tasks (per-task ratings in Appendix A.3), concentrated in the middle of the scale; this per-task survey mean is the difficulty score used in the task-sensitivity analysis below. Because the respondents are platform-internal developers rather than external practitioners, these ratings validate task realism only indicatively.

6.2Harness-Configuration Design-Validation Results

This section documents why H1b and H2b were used as the canonical H1 and H2 conditions in the main comparison. These results explain the configuration choice; the primary research-question evidence begins in Section 6.3.

The two configuration checks used A/B comparisons on T01–T05. Both compact encodings (H1b and H2b) reduced token use without an observed correctness loss on the subset. For H1, compact observation encoding used type-specific string formats that omitted null and empty fields where possible, with pipe-delimited representations for tabular outputs. H1b passed 20/35 runs, compared with 18/35 for the raw-object H1a variant. Mean total tokens fell from 334.5k to 230.3k, a 31% reduction; the final context window fell further, from 44.3k to 23.9k (46%); and estimated cost per run dropped from $0.28 to $0.18 (36%). This supports H1b as the lower-cost encoding with no observed exact-pass loss on the selection subset.

For H2, the compact variant bundled two changes: inline dictionary schemas replaced full source-style documentation, and plain dictionaries replaced typed return objects. H2b passed 33/35 runs, compared with 32/35 for H2a. Mean total tokens fell from 192.5k to 116.9k, a 39% reduction, with the final context window down 30% and estimated cost down from $0.17 to $0.12 per run (29%).

Table 6.2 reports both families side by side. The selected H1b and H2b observations for T01–T05 are also included in the 24-task main totals. The table documents the configuration choice, and from this point forward, H1 is equivalent to H1b, and H2 is equivalent to H2b.

6.3Main Harness Comparison

Table 6.3 shows the overall performance summary, per harness. H2 raises exact pass from 66/168 runs (39.29%) for H1 to 154/168 (91.67%), an increase of 88 runs and 52.38 percentage points (pp). Mean tokens fall from 329.7k to 113.2k, turns from 12.9 to 8.7, and estimated cost from $0.22 to $0.11 per run. The correctness gain comes with fewer tokens and turns. Table 6.4 shows the terminal outcomes behind this difference. H1 combines 50 wrong answers with 52 budget-bound outcomes. H2 has equal counts of wrong answers and timeouts, while H3 fails mainly through wrong answers; neither code harness reaches the turn limit.

H3 returns 153 exact answers (91.07%), one fewer than H2. It has lower descriptive means for tokens (91.8k), turns (7.9), and latency (30.8 s), with mean cost at $0.10 per run compared with H2’s $0.11. The paired analysis tests whether these changes are consistent across tasks.

Figure 6.1 shows that code execution reduces both wrong answers and budget-bound failures relative to H1. H3 times out less often than H2 but returns more wrong answers.

Table 6.5 reports the two primary comparisons, H1–H2 and H2–H3, after first aggregating the seven runs to one mean per task. It includes the headline correctness, token, context-window, latency, and turn outcomes; paired cost tests are reported with the full statistical diagnostics in Table A.1. H2 exceeds H1 on every task with a non-zero pass-rate difference, giving rank-biserial rrb​=1.000 and Holm-adjusted padj​<0.001. Tasks with identical pass rates contribute zero differences and are discarded by the signed-rank test; the effect therefore means that every differing task favours H2, not that H2 improves all 24 tasks.

The H2–H3 exact-pass difference is small and inconsistent: the median task difference is zero, rrb​=−0.194, and adjusted padj​=0.608. H3 uses fewer total tokens (rrb​=−0.513, adjusted padj​=0.027), a result qualified by the decomposition in Section 6.5.

Campaign latency falls by 5.7 s from H1 to H2 and 4.0 s from H2 to H3, but neither paired change is detected (adjusted padj​=0.900 and 0.356). Turns fall consistently only from H1 to H2 (padj​=0.007; H2–H3 padj​=0.281).

Cost per attempted run follows the same pattern as token use. As shown in Table 6.3, H1 costs $0.22 per run on average, compared with $0.11 for H2 and $0.10 for H3. This is a descriptive campaign average rather than an uncertainty-bearing estimate of future deployment cost, but it shows that H1 combines lower completion with higher resource use per attempt.

6.4Where the Differences Occur

Figure 6.2 provides the main task-level overview, alongside the two Δ columns showing H2 minus H1 and H3 minus H2.

Four tasks are solved in every run by all three harnesses: T03, T08, T18, and T24. A second group shows mainly an efficiency difference. On T02, for example, H1 succeeds in 6/7 runs and H2 and H3 in 7/7, but H1 uses 314k mean tokens against 146k for H2 and 137k for H3. For compact or report-led tasks, H1 can still pass, but at higher token cost.

On T07, T13, T14, T15, T19, and T22, H1 is 0/7 while both code harnesses are 7/7. These tasks involve graph traversal, set construction, metamodel search, or cross-source composition. T11 and T17 are similar. H1 usually invokes the platform successfully but does not complete the composition within its budgets.

The T13 traces make the contrast concrete. The task asks for org-unit/application pairs where a unit consumes an application impacted by a delayed debt item. Figure 6.3 compares the three complete model-turn traces; the full code excerpts and verifier output are reproduced in Appendix A.8. H1 returns a wrong answer after 13 turns and 249k tokens: it resolves the two delayed debt items early, then issues the required application and consuming-unit hops as six separate traverse_one_hop calls across turns 6–10, each result re-entering the conversation as a fresh observation. Without a place to hold and deduplicate the intermediate set, it submits nine pairs (recall 1.0, precision 0.56), four of them incorrect. H2 and H3 pass in eight turns and 94k/83k tokens, respectively. They query the debt items, traverse both hops, and deduplicate the pairs inside execution state, returning exactly the five expected pairs.

The trace supports the state-placement explanation, though the bundled H1–H2 contrast does not isolate it from documentation, observation flow, or error handling.

6.4.1Sensitivity of the H2–H3 Transition

H3’s one fewer pass comes from a few task-level shifts rather than a broad regression. It trails on T11, T16, T17, and T20; leads on T01, T10, T12, and T23; and ties on the other 16 tasks. The paired test detects no systematic effect (Table 6.5). The moved tasks instead show where the abstraction fits or misfits a workflow. Trace references use Txx#y for task Txx, run y; for example, H3 T16#4 is the fourth H3 run of T16.

T16 provides the clearest observed regression, by asking the agent to compare approved deployed technology products with the active standardised-products report and return the two mismatch lists in each direction. In H3 T16#4 and T16#5, the generated query retrieves all 152 technology products whose approved field is true and subtracts the standardised report. It does not apply the task’s deployed constraint. T16#4 therefore returns a large false-positive set after only six turns and 61.7k tokens. In H2 T16#4, the program explicitly reads the “Total deployed Tech Products” report, joins it by identifier with the standardised report, and passes after 11 turns and 135.3k tokens. The case shows the H3 trade-off: a concise domain query can make an under-specified selection easy and efficient while hiding the omitted scope constraint. Because much of its domain interface is focused on graph structure and traversal, H3 leaned towards graph queries, instead of relying on the user-specified reports.

The other H3 losses show related failure patterns. In H3 T11#2, the harness retrieves the criticality-5 capabilities but computes the complement over the smaller viewpoint subgraph, producing low recall. In H3 T17#4, it selects an expiring approved-products quality report rather than the report for deployed technology products ending support within one year. In H3 T20#5, it discovers both Belongs To and Owns relations between people and organisational units, but looks for organisational units that own Darryl rather than organisational units that Darryl owns. It therefore keeps only Executive Management and misses COO Office, Operations, and their applications. These failures are not mainly metamodel discovery failures: they instead concern scope, report provenance, and edge direction after a plausible abstraction has been selected.

H3’s advantages show the complementary fit. T01 and T23 benefit from domain-module functions that preserve endpoint type constraints: H3 T01#1 restricts the mitigating source to controls, while H3 T23#1 filters relationship sources to business capabilities. T10 is weaker evidence because H3 still fails two runs, but its successful runs show the domain module can carry assignment and hierarchy semantics compactly. T12 is the strongest positive trace: H3 T12#7 passes in 10 turns and 115.4k tokens, while H2 T12#3 times out after 22 turns and 362.8k tokens despite having computed the necessary intermediate data. Because H3 is still only 1/7 on T12, this is a completion example rather than a stable correctness advantage.

H3’s clearer advantage is operational: mean tokens fall from 113.2k to 91.8k, with lower total-token use on 17 of 24 tasks, and final context falls from 14.6k to 13.1k (Table 6.5). Per-run cost also falls from $0.11 for H2 to $0.10 for H3 (padj​=0.012; Table A.1), although the absolute difference is small. H3 therefore reduces total token traffic, final-context size, and model cost while giving up only one exact answer; mean latency is lower descriptively (34.8 s to 30.8 s), but the paired latency change is not detected (padj​=0.356).

6.4.2Task Characteristics

The required forms of composition from Section 2.4 help interpret the discriminating tasks but are not independent factors. T13 combines dependent typed traversal with retained intermediate identifiers; T14 and T19 construct and compare sets; T15 and T22 require metamodel discovery and local graph computation; and T07 and T17 join sizeable graph-derived collections. The observed gaps occur where several burdens co-occur, so the campaign cannot attribute a separate causal effect to any one dimension.

The overlapping tag views in Figure 6.4 provide a descriptive check. H1 has 4% mean pass on the four viewpoint tasks and 0% on the two metamodel tasks, compared with 71% and 100% for H2 and 71% and 100% for H3. H1 is stronger on report and dashboard work, where retrieved rows are generally closer to the requested answer. Component and viewpoint tasks are also costly for H1, at 447k and 407k mean tokens, compared with 157k and 206k for H2 and 100k and 130k for H3.

The technique tags in Figure 6.5 tell the same story for the better-populated groups. Across 14 graph-traversal tasks, mean pass is 30% for H1, 88% for H2, and 90% for H3; mean token use is 427k, 123k, and 96k. Across six set-difference tasks, pass is 14%, 95%, and 90%. Sparse rows such as hierarchy, set intersection, and date filter contain only one task and are case labels rather than stable category estimates. Because tags overlap, differences between rows are descriptive and cannot be interpreted as independent tag effects.

The survey-derived difficulty score does not explain much variation. Rounded to integer levels it spans only levels two through four (three, seventeen, and four tasks), giving limited spread, and its Spearman correlations with per-task pass rate and resource use are weak for every harness (∣ρ∣≤0.31), and none is significant (all p>0.15; Table A.2). Resource use trends weakly upward with difficulty for H1 and H2 but not H3, and pass rate shows no consistent association. Appendix A.2 therefore retains these diagnostics rather than using them as primary SQ3 evidence.

6.5Operational Behaviour

Figure 6.6 shows H1’s long resource tail, reaching approximately two million tokens, and the effect of the 90-second boundary on latency. Medians and interquartile ranges by outcome therefore complement means.

Table 6.6 reports resource use by terminal outcome. H1’s passing runs use a median 93.9k tokens, six turns, and 16.4 s. Its non-passing runs use 413.5k tokens, 18 turns, and 72.2 s. The split does not show that token use causes failure, because difficult tasks and long unsuccessful searches also cause more interaction. It does show that H1’s aggregate cost is driven by runs that spend much more model effort without returning an exact answer. H2 and H3 show the same direction but a much smaller gap: their non-passing median token counts are 207.5k and 104.6k.

Failed H1 traces often repeat retrieval or carry large intermediate sets across turns. This supports a high-cost failure tail; “runaway context” applies only to traces with demonstrated observation growth.

6.5.1Token Usage and the Context Window

Two token measures describe different costs. Total tokens (Table 6.7) measure cumulative traffic; the final context (Figure 6.7a) measures the last input and determines whether a workflow fits a fixed budget. H1 averages 329.7k total tokens but a 26.4k final window, so most of its traffic is context re-read turn after turn rather than newly retained state. H2 and H3 are leaner on both axes (113.2k and 91.8k total; 14.6k and 13.1k final), and their windows vary less in this campaign. H1’s final window has a standard deviation of 15.5k and reaches 97.2k on its worst run, against peaks of 35.1k and 25.2k for H2 and H3. The code-execution harnesses therefore keep individual model calls smaller and lower-peaked under the evaluated tasks and budgets.

Figure 6.7b shows how each window fills. Static prompts and documentation occupy 60–70% of the initial input. H2 and H3 peak within roughly ten to twenty turns, because each code action folds retrieval, traversal, and aggregation into one observation. H1 instead climbs gradually across as many as forty-five turns, each tool result adding to the window; this is the per-turn view of the accumulation that produces its long total-token tail.

Figure 6.8 shows how the final window is allocated. H1’s largest component is accumulated tool output, 10.3k tokens or 39% of the final window: retrieved rows and intermediate results serialised into the dialogue. Tool results are much smaller for H2 and H3, at 2.7k and 2.4k tokens, around 19% each, because intermediate state can remain in the sandbox. Tool definitions are instead their largest component, at 7.1k tokens (48%) for H2 and 6.1k (46%) for H3. The model’s emitted call arguments are a separate component, close to 10% of the window for H2 and H3 but only 4% for H1, while user messages are negligible throughout. Retained model reasoning is a further 4.5k tokens (17%) for H1 and 2.8k and 2.9k (19% and 22%) for H2 and H3, and the static system prompt is a small fixed remainder near 0.5k.

6.5.2Latency

Model inference dominates mean latency: 97% for H1, 98% for H2, and 93% for H3 (Figure 6.9). H3 spends more recorded tool time than H2 (2.2s versus 0.7s) because domain operations hide more work inside each action. The 90-second boundary shapes H1’s slow tail.

Neither paired latency difference is detected, as shown in Table 6.5. H3’s lower mean is therefore a campaign average, not evidence that every task is faster. Among runs that avoid timeout and turn exhaustion, H1 averages 19.6 s, compared with 32.2 s for H2. This subset excludes the long H1 failures at the operating boundary, so it should not be read as evidence that H1 is generally faster.

Generated source is also only a diagnostic. Per execute_code call, H3 produces less Python source than H2, with 12.1 ± 7.9 total lines compared with 13.9 ± 10.0 for H2. This is consistent with recurring coordination being encoded in reusable operations. Source length does not measure implementation complexity, cognitive effort, hidden platform work, or maintainability, and is therefore not used as a headline benefit.

6.6Failure Behaviour

Failure analysis separates terminal outcomes, execution events, partial-answer quality, and interpretation. H1 averages only 0.10 malformed calls and 0.10 framework retries per run. Its 102 non-passing runs are therefore not primarily schema-validation failures. For H2 and H3, sandbox events are uncommon and usually recoverable. As Table 6.8 shows, six of eight H2 runs with runtime errors still pass, as do all eleven such H3 runs.

Table 6.9 restricts partial credit to failed collection answers. H1’s mean recall (0.92) is much higher than its precision (0.69), with 3.27 extra items and 0.88 missing items on average. Its typical collection failure is therefore more often over-inclusion than loss of the last expected items. The pattern is especially visible on T13, T16, T17, and T23, where failed H1 runs often retain recall of 1.0 while including irrelevant components. The extra and missing item counts for H3 were heavily inflated by a few badly wrong answers.

H2 has only seven eligible failed collection runs, so its similar aggregate precision and recall have a small denominator. H3’s 13 eligible failures are more heterogeneous. T16 failures have recall 1.0 but very low precision because the missing deployment constraint admits a large product set. In contrast, the failed T11 and T17 runs under-retrieve relevant capabilities or technology products. This mixture produces lower mean precision and recall and very large variance in extra and missing counts. The result does not show when a partial answer would be useful in practice; it diagnoses the direction of error under the strict exact-pass contract.

Every failing run also carries a post-hoc self-reflection in which the agent names a probable failure cause. These reports record how the agent perceives a run from inside the loop, not a verified diagnosis; the verifier remains the only ground truth, and they are read here as the agent’s perspective on its own failures rather than as evidence of their causes. Manual trace inspection found that the reports often aligned with the observed issue, but this alignment was not coded as a separate measure. Their content differs systematically by harness; Appendix A.7 (Table A.9) lists representative examples for each.

Figure 6.10 shows their distribution. Across all three harnesses the most common self-perceived cause is incomplete data (46% of H1 failures, 57% for H2, 60% for H3): even the code-execution harnesses, on the rare runs they fail, more often read the failure as missing information than as a flawed method. “Wrong approach” is the next most frequent category (28% for H1, 14% for H2, 40% for H3). H3’s larger share is consistent with the semantic-selection shortcut documented for the T12 boundary case (Section 6.6.1), where the agent matches on a supplier name instead of following the supplier relation.

“Too many results” appears only under H1 (11% of its failing runs) and never under H2 or H3. None of these eleven runs submitted an over-inclusive answer that the verifier rejected; all reached the time or turn budget first (nine timeouts and two turn-limit terminations) while still expanding an over-broad traversal. Their reflections describe the same shape: a multi-hop expansion that requires many sequential per-entity lookups, including one call per person and per unit, one per at-risk application, and a stack with “300+ Deploys To targets”, which cannot be completed within the limit. The label therefore marks budget exhaustion during over-broad retrieval, the serial-call cost of holding and growing the working set in conversation, rather than a submitted answer with too many items. It is the same tendency that, when an answer is returned, surfaces as over-inclusion in the verifier (Table 6.9: H1 precision 0.69 against recall 0.92, with 3.27 extra items on average): one cause, expressed either as a run that never finishes or as an answer that over-includes. The remaining categories (conflicting data, unexpected data shape, tool errors, and data not found) are individually rare and occur almost only under H1. The self-reports broadly track the measured failure modes, but they remain unvalidated and are not used as causal evidence.

6.6.1The T12 Boundary Case

T12 asks which applications integrate with at least one SAP-supplied application in the application integration map, and which business capabilities those integrating applications realise.

All harnesses have a valid solution path for T12, yet only one of 21 runs passes. H1 and H2 fail all seven runs, while H3 passes once and fails six times. The traces show different reasons for failure rather than an impossible verifier.

In H1 T12#1, the agent first finds nine applications by matching the supplier name, then corrects this shortcut by resolving the supplier organisation and following Supplies to all eleven applications. It continues interpreting the application–interface–application graph through serial calls and reaches the timeout without submitting an answer. In H2 T12#3, generated code obtains the same eleven supplied applications, reconstructs the exact nine integrating applications, and retrieves the exact ten realised capabilities. The run then times out before returning its typed final result. This is a completion failure despite the necessary data having been computed.

H3 exhibits a different recurrent failure. In H3 T12#1, it selects applications whose names contain the supplier string rather than following the supplier relationship. This omits two supplied applications whose names do not contain the string, misclassifies one of them as an external integrator, and changes the downstream capability set. Five completed H3 wrong answers repeat this same shortcut, although H3 T12#7 follows a valid path and passes. The task therefore exposes both budget exhaustion during graph interpretation and semantic selection error. Harness design helps with the former but does not guarantee correct interpretation of the supplier relation.

As Table 6.10 reports, excluding T12 raises pass rates to 40.99%, 95.65%, and 94.41% and lowers mean tokens without changing the ranking or conclusions.

6.7Discussion

Paired task analysis shows whether differences repeat across tasks; task groups and traces suggest mechanisms. Taken together, the results show that harness architecture affects performance by changing where intermediate state, coordination, and domain semantics live.

6.7.1SQ1: Stateful Composition and Execution Responsibility

H2 improves correctness and efficiency together, especially on compositional tasks. H1’s low malformed-call rate rules out schema validation as the main explanation. The more plausible mechanism is state placement: H1 repeatedly serialises dependent work through the dialogue, while H2 retains identifiers and performs joins or aggregation in Python before returning a compact result.

Several diagnostics support this interpretation and weaken alternative explanations. H1 averages only 0.10 malformed calls and 0.10 framework retries per run, so its 102 non-passing runs are rarely invalid JSON calls. Its failed collection answers are also not simple non-retrieval failures: their mean recall is 0.92, while precision is 0.69, indicating frequent over-inclusion after substantial relevant retrieval. The context-window breakdown points to the same mechanism. H1 retains 10.3k tokens of tool results in the final window, compared with 2.7k for H2, because intermediate rows, identifiers, and partial sets re-enter the conversation. H2 can keep those values in execution state and print only selected summaries or final projections.

The task evidence follows the same pattern. T13 illustrates the mechanism in one trace, while the broader gains on traversal, set construction, metamodel lookup, and cross-source composition show that the effect is not trace-specific. This interpretation agrees with work on executable control flow [46, 14] and conversational state dependence [45]. SQ1 therefore supports the realised programmatic harness: executable state, local data structures, compact printed observations, and recoverable execution errors.

The implication is not merely to replace JSON with Python. It is to give dependent work a bounded execution environment where values can be retained and transformed without repeated conversational mediation. The corresponding cost is an infrastructure responsibility: isolation, inspection, limits, recovery, and observability become part of the harness.

6.7.2SQ2: Semantic Abstraction and Governance Responsibility

H3 changes how the agent works more than how well it does. It returns one fewer exact answer than H2, a difference the paired test does not detect (padj​=0.608, median task difference zero) and that could be run-to-run variation, while total tokens and final context fall consistently across tasks. Per-run model cost also falls from $0.11 to $0.10 on average, with a paired median task difference of −$0.0095 (padj​=0.012), while mean latency falls from 34.8 s to 30.8 s without a detected paired change (padj​=0.356). The notable effect is not the single missing answer but the change in failure composition: H3 reaches the budget far less often than H2 (one timeout against seven) yet returns more wrong answers (fourteen against seven). The abstraction makes the agent more decisive, completing compositions that H2 leaves running, while sometimes committing to a selection assumption that a lower-level program would have kept open to question.

This mixed result matches evidence that abstraction level is a performance lever, not a monotonic improvement [57, 16]. The H3 result is consistent with higher-level skills reducing token traffic, but it does not show that higher abstraction generally improves reliability. In this campaign, abstraction reduced total tokens and final context while leaving exact pass statistically indistinguishable from H2 and shifting the failures toward semantic mistakes.

The trace evidence separates two kinds of semantic responsibility. H3 helps when a domain-module function preserves endpoint-type, relationship-source, or hierarchy semantics that generated code would otherwise need to rediscover, as in T01, T23, and the successful H3 run on T12. It hurts when the selected operation, report, or traversal fixes the wrong scope, provenance, direction, or selection rule, as in T16, T17, T20, and the repeated T12 supplier-name shortcut. The central issue is therefore governance of abstraction boundaries. Once semantics move into maintained code, correctness depends on names, operation scope, validation rules, examples, and escape routes back to lower level inspection. The experiment did not detect a systematic correctness difference, but 24 tasks do not establish equivalence between H2 and H3. SQ2 therefore supports H3 when reusable, governed domain-module functions justify transferring semantic responsibility into maintained code: its value is leaner interaction and reuse at minimal correctness cost, not a correctness upgrade over H2.

6.7.3SQ3: Task Sensitivity

The largest harness differences occur on graph traversal, metamodel analysis, set construction, cross-report comparison, and viewpoint-based composition. These tasks require several of the compositional burdens introduced in Section 2.4 at once: dependent calls, retained intermediate identifiers, local computation, schema discovery, and choice among platform abstraction layers. H1 remains adequate on several compact report, dashboard, and aggregation tasks where the platform already returns data close to the final answer.

The task results separate three workflow regimes. In direct or asset-led retrieval, such as dashboards, compact reports, and some aggregations, the benefit of code execution is smaller because the retrieved asset already resembles the answer. In stateful composition, including graph traversal, set-difference, metamodel, and cross-report work, H2 and H3 dominate because they can retain identifiers, branch over collections, and compute locally. In semantically loaded abstraction, where correctness depends on relationship direction, report provenance, viewpoint scope, or component-type constraints, H3 can either preserve the intended semantics or make a wrong shortcut cheaper to execute.

The tag views support these regimes without making the tags causal factors. H1 has 4% mean pass on viewpoint tasks and 0% on metamodel tasks, compared with 71% and 100% for both code harnesses. Across graph-traversal tasks, mean pass is 30% for H1, 88% for H2, and 90% for H3; across set-difference tasks, it is 14%, 95%, and 90%. These rows overlap and some contain few tasks, but they show where the aggregate result comes from. T12 marks the boundary for the H2–H3 transition: H3’s single successful run shows that a domain module can reduce enough orchestration to complete a difficult composition, while the remaining failures show that abstraction still cannot ensure correct interpretation or timely completion.

SQ3 therefore answers the main research question in structural terms. Harness architecture affects performance by deciding which coordination remains probabilistic and conversational, which state and computation become executable, and which domain semantics are embedded in reusable code. It can reduce coordination burden, but it cannot eliminate semantic interpretation or completion risk.

6.7.4Practical Implications

The empirical and engineering implications are asymmetric. Moving from H1 to H2 adds sandboxing, generated-code inspection, documentation, retry handling, and timeout controls. The benchmark nevertheless gives strong evidence that this infrastructure is worthwhile for the evaluated compositional workflows. Moving from H2 to H3 adds operation design, validation logic, normalised return structures, and abstraction governance. Its justification depends more on reuse and organisational control than on a general empirical advantage.

The practical sequence follows the same pattern. H1 fits narrow workflows when direct calls are sufficient, when each platform action should remain explicitly visible in the conversation, or when code-execution infrastructure is not justified. H2 is the stronger default for multi-step analytical workflows when sandboxing and generated-code inspection are acceptable. H3 should be adopted more selectively: it is most defensible when recurring analyses justify maintained domain operations and when the organisation can govern their names, assumptions, validation rules, documentation, and low-level escape routes. A domain module that hides too much can make the agent faster at the wrong interpretation.

Table 6.11 separates measured results from engineering work that was not evaluated. The guidance is scoped to analytical queries; write operations, approval gates, human usability, and production governance were not evaluated.

6.7.5Threats to Validity and Generalisability

The detailed validity account is given in Section 4.8. The main boundary for these findings is that each harness is an implemented condition, not a single isolated design variable. Provided results are also scoped to this single case-study.

The results also depend on the benchmark setting: one model route, one seeded Ardoq deployment, one implementation of each harness, and 24 analytical tasks. Exact pass measures agreement with the oracle, not explanation quality or procedure quality. Task tags and difficulty scores locate patterns but do not identify causal task attributes. H3 internal work is less observable than H2 wrapped calls, so comparisons rely on model-visible actions and run-level resources rather than symmetric platform-operation counts. The A/B studies justify the compact H1 and H2 variants used in the main comparison, but they are design-validation checks on a five-task subset rather than independent confirmation of SQ1 or SQ2. The T12 exclusion shows that the headline ranking does not depend on one boundary case, but it does not remove the limits of the fixed benchmark.

Table 6.12 consolidates the finding, primary evidence, and claim boundary for each research question. Within these boundaries, the evidence supports H2 as the strongest default for the evaluated compositional workflows and H3 as a selective abstraction trade-off rather than a correctness upgrade. The main research question can therefore be answered as follows: harness architecture changes Ardoq-agent behaviour by allocating work among the conversation, execution state, and maintained domain code. The largest observed gain comes from moving stateful composition out of the conversation. Raising the same execution model to a domain module mainly reduces interaction cost and changes failure composition, rather than improving exact correctness.
chap:conclusion:
This thesis treated the agent–platform interface as a performance-bearing architectural variable and located three concrete harnesses in a two-dimensional design space of invocation style and abstraction level (Figure 2.7). H1 uses traditional tool calling over low-level operations; H2 keeps those operations but moves invocation into code execution; H3 keeps code execution but raises the operations to an agent-native domain module. The staged comparison is organised around two axes: H1–H2 changes invocation style and state placement, while H2–H3 changes abstraction level over a shared execution model. The controlled study compared the three on 24 read-only Ardoq tasks, with seven runs per task–harness cell and typed live-API oracles.

Within this space, the clearest result came from the change in invocation style, not the change in abstraction level. Moving dependent work into an executable environment improved completion and efficiency together; raising that same environment to a domain module made the interaction leaner with little change in correctness. The harness governs how work is divided among the model, the conversation, the runtime, and reusable domain code, and that division is where the measured differences came from.

7.1Answer to the Research Question

SQ1—invocation style. Replacing H1 with H2 produced the largest and most consistent effect. Exact pass rose from 39.29% to 91.67% and mean tokens fell from 329.7k to 113.2k, with fewer turns and no turn-limit outcomes; every non-zero task-level difference favoured H2. The gaps concentrated on graph traversal, set construction, metamodel analysis, and cross-source composition, tasks where H1 repeatedly serialised intermediate values through the conversation while H2 retained and transformed them in code. SQ1 supports the implemented programmatic harness as a bundle, not code syntax isolated from state, documentation, and observation flow.

SQ2—abstraction level. Replacing H2’s low-level functions with the H3 domain module changed how the agent worked more than how well it did. Exact pass fell by one run (153 versus 154 of 168, padj​=0.608), while total tokens fell from 113.2k to 91.8k, with lower total-token use on 17 of 24 tasks, and final context fell from 14.6k to 13.1k. Cost followed the same direction, falling from $0.11 to $0.10 per run (padj​=0.012). Latency should be read more cautiously: H3’s mean was lower than H2’s (30.8 s versus 34.8 s), but the paired task comparison did not support a reliable latency reduction (padj​=0.356). The abstraction bought compaction at little correctness cost, not a correctness gain. Its failures also shifted in kind: H3 reached the budget far less often than H2 but returned more wrong answers, so the module made the agent more decisive while roughly maintaining accuracy, completing compositions that H2 left running while sometimes committing to an under-specified interpretation. Task-level gains, where a domain operation preserved type or hierarchy semantics, roughly offset losses, where an operation or report fixed the wrong scope, provenance, or edge direction. Twenty-four tasks do not establish equivalence, but within this study the module delivered leaner interaction for a one-run drop in exact pass.

SQ3—task sensitivity. The differences tracked workflow structure. H1 stayed competitive when reports, dashboards, or aggregations returned data close to the answer, and weakened when tasks combined dependent retrieval, retained identifiers, local computation, and schema discovery. Overlapping tags and survey-derived difficulty make these descriptive rather than causal task effects.

7.2Contributions

The thesis makes four contributions.

  1. An architectural framing and controlled empirical comparison. The study treats the harness as a performance-bearing variable and stages two interpretable transitions within one platform. Programmatic composition improved completion and efficiency; the agent-native domain module then reduced interaction traffic at minimal correctness cost.

  2. An objectively verifiable enterprise architecture benchmark. The 24-task suite translates analytical Ardoq workflows into typed contracts and trajectory-independent live-API oracles. It covers the platform’s main query, traversal, and metamodel operations while permitting different valid solution paths, requiring retrieval and computation that can inform professional EA judgement without automating it. Additionally, a human expert survey confirms the real-life applicability of the created tasks. The proprietary code and seeded deployment make it an internal research artefact.

  3. A repeated-trial evaluation methodology. The pipeline combines exact verification with task-paired analysis, resource telemetry, terminal outcomes, partial-answer diagnostics, and auditable traces, characterising stochastic variation while separating verified outcomes from observed mechanics and trace interpretations.

  4. Bounded guidance for enterprise agent-interface design. The evidence consolidates into a conditional selection framework (Table 6.11) that ties each harness to the workflow structure and engineering commitment it suits, rather than a single ranking. It also provides actionable insight into the design of H1 and H2, both applicable to production deployments at Ardoq, by empirically comparing A/B variations of each.

Together, the contributions connect harness architecture to measured behaviour on a schema-governed enterprise platform, and the benchmark and pipeline support later harness tests under the same verification method.

7.3Practical Implications

Code execution is an architectural investment, not a formatting convenience. For iteration, joins, aggregation, graph traversal, or schema search, it keeps intermediate data outside the conversation and supplies ordinary programming constructs. These benefits must be weighed against isolation, code inspection, timeouts, retries, credential boundaries, and observability. Short report-led workflows may not justify that infrastructure.

For organisations facing the workflow types evaluated here, the practical sequence is to retain H1 for narrow, direct interactions, adopt H2 as the default for compositional analysis when code execution is operationally acceptable, and invest in H3 only when stable recurring operations justify the additional abstraction-governance cost. In this campaign, estimated model cost per successful run was approximately $0.56 for H1, $0.12 for H2, and $0.11 for H3. These figures exclude the engineering and operating costs of sandboxing, security controls, observability, and domain-module maintenance.

An agent-native domain module transfers coordination and semantic assumptions into maintained platform code. This can improve compactness, but makes abstraction design part of product governance. Enterprise architects and governance stakeholders may help define stable concepts, permitted operations, validation, report-selection rules, directionality guarantees, and audit requirements. Because the benchmark did not evaluate human usability or governance, this remains an implementation implication.

7.4Scope of the Conclusions

These conclusions cover three implemented harnesses, one frontier model, one seeded Ardoq deployment, fixed budgets, and 24 read-only tasks. The deployment contains rich solution assets but no live customer records. Mutation, approval workflows, concurrent users, external integrations, and sustained production operation remain untested, and other models, datasets, and platforms may behave differently.

The staged design compares complete harnesses rather than independently isolating syntax, state, documentation, observation flow, validation, or abstraction. It also does not quantify implementation effort, maintenance, security, auditability, or human oversight. The result is a bounded architectural choice, not a universal ordering or claim of production readiness.

7.5Future Work

The design space points to the most direct extension. The three harnesses occupy three of its four corners (from Figure 2.7); the missing one is high-level domain operations exposed through traditional tool calling rather than code execution. Building it would vary abstraction within the tool-calling style and isolate whether H3’s compaction came from the domain abstraction or from the move to code execution. It would also show what tool definitions result once domain operations have to be expressed as discrete calls rather than a code module.

Beyond the missing corner, the priority is replication across model families, platforms, datasets, and independently constructed task suites, to test whether the H1–H2 result generalises beyond Ardoq and whether models benefit equally from execution state. Replications should retain paired tasks and repeated runs while adding prompt perturbations and controlled infrastructure failures.

H3 is one point in a larger design space, and several directions could improve it. The most direct is to widen the module by adding operations, so that more common analyses are served by a single domain call rather than assembled by hand. The module could also be built on a different programming paradigm, such as a more object-oriented or a more functional one, to test which style the model uses more reliably. A larger change is to move away from low-level primitives and encode workflows directly: instead of exposing the building blocks of an analysis, the module would expose the analysis itself. Each of these choices raises a question the study leaves open, namely how to design the SDK well and where an abstraction becomes too abstract, hiding so much that the model can no longer tell what an operation will do. Further out, the agent could maintain the module itself and form a complete feedback loop. As it answers user queries, it would add new operations or revise existing ones to match the questions it encounters, either during a run or afterwards, so the module grows in step with how the platform is actually used.

Production-oriented evaluation should add write permissions, approval gates, rollback, and state restoration, with procedure-aware verification that checks data sources, traversal constraints, provenance, and prohibited shortcuts alongside final answers. Longitudinal and multi-user studies could then measure drift, concurrency, recovery, and oversight. Cost is the other open variable: the campaign priced model usage but left out sandbox operation, security controls, observability, interface maintenance, and the governance each domain abstraction requires, with documentation drift a recurring cost specific to H3 whose value depends on its descriptions still matching the platform they wrap. A full accounting would show whether the leaner interaction of H2 and H3 holds once the supporting infrastructure is counted.

7.6Closing Perspective

Agent capability depends on the interface through which the model observes, composes, and executes work. In this study, the transition that kept dependent operations and intermediate values in an executable environment produced the clearest gain; adding a domain abstraction made interaction leaner while barely affecting correctness. A harness allocates work among the model, context, runtime, and domain code. That allocation is a first-class architectural decision.

This matters beyond Ardoq. As organisations move LLMs from pilots into the systems where work actually happens, the value they capture will depend less on the model alone than on how it is connected to applications, data models, permissions, and procedures. The interface decides which work the model reasons through token by token and which it offloads to code or to the platform, and that choice affects not only whether a task succeeds but what it costs to run. The question does not fade as models improve. A more capable model still acts through some interface, and a better one frees that capability for the parts of a problem that genuinely need judgement.

The agent-native direction pushes this further, asking what an interface would look like if it were designed for the agent rather than inherited from human developers. This thesis gives one controlled answer, on one platform, rather than a general theory. What it shows is that the harness is where enterprise agents can be made more capable and more efficient, and that designing it well deserves the same care as the choice of model and data.
